For years, conservatives who said they were being cut off from the banking system were dismissed as paranoid. Now the Treasury Department has confirmed it. On October 14, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Treasury bureau that regulates national banks, [released the findings](https://substack.com/redirect/00acc7dd-e5ed-4c55-ae00-3e47281d5cd1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) of its review of the nation's nine largest banks. All nine had policies between 2020 and September 2025 that could deny or limit financial services to Americans based on their political or religious beliefs or their lawful business activities. The banks were:
* JPMorgan Chase
* Bank of America
* Citibank
* Wells Fargo
* U.S. Bank
* Capital One
* PNC Bank
* TD Bank
* BMO Bank

| [](https://substack.com/redirect/cc5215a8-2fdf-42a5-b337-fcf5cabb8a9b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
The OCC found that vague "reputation risk" policies with no objective standards were used to disadvantage Americans because of their political, religious, or social views. The banks also kept public and secret policies cutting off entire lawful industries - oil and gas, coal, firearms and ammunition, detention facilities, tobacco and e-cigarettes, and digital assets. The list shows that these institutions targeted President Trump, his supporters, and conservative-leaning organizations.
The findings came from a review of nearly 100,000 complaints and roughly 50,000 internal bank documents totaling some 420,000 pages. Comptroller Jonathan Gould called it "irrefutable evidence that the nation's largest banks have denied, debanked and discriminated against customers."
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/30e52f78-5369-44c6-9344-6964fa2b74bc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
This wasn't just Wall Street acting on its own. As Heritage Foundation economist E.J. Antoni [pointed out](https://substack.com/redirect/75c0a70b-cb3b-40ef-98f7-2603407570ae?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), the OCC's own findings show Washington leaning on the banks. A Wells Fargo review cited "greater supervisory pressure" under the Biden administration to move away from firearms lending. Another bank dropped private-prison clients over "changing policymaker attitudes." JPMorgan's WePay closed a merchant selling MAGA merchandise, and its screening flagged the phrase "America First." Bank examiners graded institutions on "reputational risk" - a category with no financial definition that let regulators punish disfavored customers, like Republicans, without ever having to justify it.
Laura Loomer knows this firsthand. On February 19, 2019, she opened her Chase app to find an "Access Suspended" notice. As Loomered.com [reported at the time](https://substack.com/redirect/89b27531-c018-4997-8d26-19d30d35f3b4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), she called the bank and went to a branch with two forms of ID, and Chase still refused to restore her access or explain why. PayPal had cut her off just two weeks earlier, and Chase was closing the accounts of other conservative activists at the same time. Only after the story went national did a Chase executive office employee call to say the accounts would be reinstated - again with no explanation as to why they were suspended to begin with.
She has warned for years that JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon led the effort to debank conservatives and Trump supporters:
[| | | | | Laura Loomer
---
@LauraLoomer
Over the last decade, Jamie Dimon, the CEO of JPMorgan Chase @jpmorgan has led efforts to debank conservatives, Trump supporters, and individuals like myself. My online banking at Chase was actually once shut down by Chase Bank, in an act of political targeting in 2019. I ...
| 11:59 PM * Aug 1, 2025 * 385K Views299 Replies * 2.4K Reposts * 6.63K Likes
---](https://substack.com/redirect/a3fdcaf5-5c62-4e22-aa7d-c1b74c78aeac?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
For that, she was called a conspiracy theorist. Now the federal government's own bank regulator has confirmed what she was saying all along.
The banks weren't the only ones doing it. Debanking was one front in a much broader campaign by the Biden administration against conservatives.

The Justice Department's Weaponization Working Group [found in August](https://substack.com/redirect/0be0a9e4-a559-4a3e-bc37-02469e873330?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) that the Biden FBI's Richmond Field Office "associated beliefs held by many Catholics with domestic extremism," relied on Southern Poverty Law Center smears, and investigated and monitored two priests - only to find "no link to criminal activity or violent extremism." The SPLC is a far-left organization that is currently being brought to court for funding some of the very groups it was meant to oppose, essentially creating a boogeyman so it could keep fat fundraising checks coming in.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/c0b4d8bd-6f63-4b48-aa47-3c19f47c71b0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
This month, the same group [revealed](https://substack.com/redirect/77679a0b-303c-4c8d-b637-008b45dc7ed6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) that the Biden White House pressed Merrick Garland's DOJ to go after parents who protested at school board meetings. The FBI opened 25 threat assessments on parents, none of which led to a single prosecution, and one of Garland's own deputies warned it would make the department look like an "Anti-MAGA Task Force."
Add in [Operation Arctic Frost](https://substack.com/redirect/236daa79-2f60-4931-8981-230d05b408cf?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), which Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley says targeted more than a dozen members of Congress and over 400 Republican organizations and individuals, and the picture is complete: if you were a conservative under Biden, the government was coming for your bank account, your church, your kids' school board, and your phone records.
We know all of this only because of President Trump's [executive order](https://substack.com/redirect/b8cc78e2-56d9-4c8c-856c-ef0156d42b3a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), "Guaranteeing Fair Access to Banking for All Americans." If President Trump hadn't won in 2024, these banks would still be quietly closing the accounts of honest Americans for the crime of being honest Americans.
Some will say this is all in the past - that "woke 1.0" is over and corporate America has moved on. That's what AOC and her friends [want](https://substack.com/redirect/b885c03e-0c30-4ae7-8eb4-3d18b545ab0f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) you to think. There is no such thing as woke 1.0. The policies, the people who wrote them, and the culture that produced them are still there. The OCC found these practices running until September 2025, well into President Trump's second term. The banks have quietly scrubbed some of their policies, but Gould himself said he is "not confident" those efforts "will be enough."
Neither is Loomer Unleashed.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/af3ba809-2b6a-44cd-b1ac-19bed71f5d72?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
The people who built this system are still being rewarded for it. Laura Loomer sounded the alarm last year when the White House picked a lawyer who had defended Citibank and Bank of America in court - after they cut off gun manufacturers - to run the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission:

For years, conservatives who said they were being cut off from the banking system were dismissed as paranoid. Now the Treasury Department has confirmed it. On October 14, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Treasury bureau that regulates national banks, of its review of the nation's nine largest banks. All nine had policies between 2020 and September 2025 that could deny or limit financial services to Americans based on their political or religious beliefs or their lawful business activities. The banks were: JPMorgan Chase Bank of America Citibank Wells Fargo U.S. Bank Capital One PNC Bank TD Bank * BMO Bank | | ---|---|--- The OCC found that vague "reputation risk" policies with no objective standards were used to disadvantage Americans because of their political, religious, or social views. The banks also kept public and secret policies cutting off entire lawful industries - oil and gas, coal, firearms and ammunition, detention facilities, tobacco and e-cigarettes, and digital assets. The list shows that these institutions targeted President Trump, his supporters, and conservative-leaning organizations. The findings came from a review of nearly 100,000 complaints and roughly 50,000 internal bank documents totaling some 420,000 pages. Comptroller Jonathan Gould called it "irrefutable evidence that the nation's largest banks have denied, debanked and discriminated against customers." | | ---|---|--- This wasn't just Wall Street acting on its own. As Heritage Foundation economist E.J. Antoni , the OCC's own findings show Washington leaning on the banks. A Wells Fargo review cited "greater supervisory pressure" under the Biden administration to move away from firearms lending. Another bank dropped private-prison clients over "changing policymaker attitudes." JPMorgan's WePay closed a merchant selling MAGA merchandise, and its screening flagged the phrase "America First." Bank examiners graded institutions on "reputational risk" - a category with no financial definition that let regulators punish disfavored customers, like Republicans, without ever having to justify it. Laura Loomer knows this firsthand. On February 19, 2019, she opened her Chase app to find an "Access Suspended" notice. As Loomered.com , she called the bank and went to a branch with two forms of ID, and Chase still refused to restore her access or explain why. PayPal had cut her off just two weeks earlier, and Chase was closing the accounts of other conservative activists at the same time. Only after the story went national did a Chase executive office employee call to say the accounts would be reinstated - again with no explanation as to why they were suspended to begin with. She has warned for years that JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon led the effort to debank conservatives and Trump supporters: For that, she was called a conspiracy theorist. Now the federal government's own bank regulator has confirmed what she was saying all along. The banks weren't the only ones doing it. Debanking was one front in a much broader campaign by the Biden administration against conservatives. LOOMER UNLEASHED is a reader-supported publication. The SPLC is a far-left organization that is currently being brought to court for funding some of the very groups it was meant to oppose, essentially creating a boogeyman so it could keep fat fundraising checks coming in. | | ---|---|--- This month, the same group that the Biden White House pressed Merrick Garland's DOJ to go after parents who protested at school board meetings. name: Roy Cooper
subject: My decision to swing for the fences
body:
I'm betting on this team, Peter.
| [](https://act.roycooper.com/go/15912?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1755&source=&t=1&akid=5180%2E124072%2EXiaONx) | | | |
---
Peter,
We were running out of time to reach the voters we needed to win this race, so I made a risky decision: I approved our final ad spend even though we didn’t have the budget for it yet.
It’s the only way we’d be able to keep our message in front of voters up until the very end. However, now we’re in a very tough spot, and I need your urgent help to make up the difference. **We’re due to send out our final wire of the campaign at 5 p.m., so please:**
[**_If you’ve been waiting for the best moment to chip in your first donation to my campaign, THIS is it. Will you give what you can?_**](https://act.roycooper.com/go/15912?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1755&amount=5&t=8&akid=5180%2E124072%2EXiaONx)
Elections in North Carolina are notorious for coming down to razor-thin margins no matter what the polls and predictions say. That’s why we simply can’t leave anything to chance.
The GOP has poured tens of millions into this race to defeat me, and President Trump has come to NC multiple times to rally alongside my opponent, Michael Whatley. They know as well as we do that if we lose NC, Democrats will lose the Senate.
**I took a leap of faith when I OK’d the new ad spend so we could reach millions more voters with our message – but now, I need people like you to have my back.**
[**_Please, Peter, this is important. Will you chip in $5 or even just a few bucks to help me close this budget gap, win in North Carolina and take back the Senate?_**](https://act.roycooper.com/go/15912?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1755&amount=5&t=9&akid=5180%2E124072%2EXiaONx)
Grateful to have you with me in this fight.
Roy Cooper
_If you've donated via check, mail or in-person event, thank you! Our system may not have processed your gift yet, but rest assured, we have received it. Please note, if you have given through a spouse or another email or phone number, our records may not have transferred that information here. We are grateful for your support and no further action is required at this time._
| |
* * *
[](https://act.roycooper.com/go/15912?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1755&t=2&akid=5180%2E124072%2EXiaONx)
Democrat Roy Cooper is running for U.S. Senate to help take back the Majority for Democrats. North Carolina is Democrats’ best chance to flip a seat from red to blue — the path to stopping Republicans in Washington starts here.

National Republicans will target North Carolina as a key battleground and invest heavily in defeating us.

Cooper is a former state legislator, Attorney General, and most recently Governor of North Carolina. North Carolina will be the most competitive Senate election of 2026, and Cooper enters the race as the most formidable candidate of either party.

Cooper’s signature achievements include helping to expand Medicaid and helping make NC the top state for business by creating thousands of jobs and growing the clean energy economy.

Polk was [born](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJyk0D-O6yAQgPHT4C4WM-B_BcVr3OW1W1oEhni0GEdm4ii3X2WvsBf46dP3dV2unjOX-3-_kRNJS6FXzSRCxyIsvtTkc-ayn3QIb-StftOCGvsLwEXj4oPwSYv1TXQ3hMnb0JCDYTI9DAPaZnXJjBam6JMeIYUQg0aDozFo9egxQcPuAwJoBNCjxfZG1GkaPJho9dQlZTVFlv1oZSWhUqhWopTfn6w27FuT3SryqMr8UzgrnNfYrvuzUuSTI8U2cvjmUvfSUnwqnMseSeFs-s5Ac7j4eHHOXPtBWX3fPOdfVf645HT4EwAA__-YAXUK) in North Carolina. His family moved to Tennessee in 1806, and he went on to become Speaker of the U.S. House, governor of Tennessee, and the 11th president. A Hermitage father and daughter brought [Showbiz Pizza Place](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJykkLGupDAMRb8mdBklJgM7BcU2dG_bLZEBh1gbEpT4DZr5-hWj_YPtbB3LOvf-_pq-kCOn7RfuNIj4KdFZI4lQmYQFU_UYI6f8pCK8EzrzogkMdNpabWDCRfhJk8NmHWawD3RLQ4PtH21n-x5cEwZC77BtPd1hBTMvHtq7BeoczM50fm14uB5aa8Ba88PBbSa6G-rRtqszj7tXztDKkstNAgmlRLUS-fi6tG5L3ps4BJGjqvanglHBeJ7n7fxT0gUVjFcqBWPMC0b9b0lYw5NjJAVjoLKz4EbaowQqesXvLcg1fGedD0pVb1g-B7nogDHmkyjpGvI581sf_H6jPiIupDHxjlJy4uXDFYxNGdbj5Bi5dr1yZtuR40dc_rP15wB_AwAA__8tRpu0) animatronics back to life in their garage on Halloween night. Read about it in _Et Cetera_ , and hit reply to tell us where you celebrated birthdays as a kid. The clocks fell back this weekend, and almost nobody is happy about it. But ending the time change is harder than it sounds. America tried going without it once, and what happened that winter turned the whole country around in a matter of weeks. Fifty years later, the fight is back on, so how did we end up changing our clocks in the first place, and is this the year it finally stops? On today's episode of _Flyover Focus_ , we dig into the strange history of Daylight Saving Time, the 1974 experiment that changed everything, and the three ways this could all end. ## Strong Early Turnout before Tuesday's Vote
More than 1.28 million Tennesseans [voted early](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJykkDGO6zAMRE8jdzEkWrGSQsVv3OW3WxoyRScEaDmwuDFy-4VT7AW2JYE3b-brNt4SC5f7_7RQVJ3HQnsVUqVtVNZU6pxEuKwv2pQXSt6-aQQL_cm5k4UxofKLRp-aHCdw1-SxoejCtetdCOCbR4QL-h5ytilnDKGjC-TunCZEtHYCbDgeQOcsOGcvHtqJ6GwpJNdlb6_n2XhLmXXdWn2QUilUK9Es70OrxXVpJD5Un9V0_wwMBoZ939sy4dHm-BsYnquwMlYDw0efhFB5LcfhF3naqH6L1maL-bmzCNc-GG_vS2L5BOkfV3pF-AkAAP__xJl9sg) or by mail ahead of Tuesday's election, about 27% of the state's 4.78 million registered voters. That's well ahead of the [2022 midterm pace](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJykkLGO8yAQhJ8Gd0SwISYuKP7GXf72SmsNS4KEIYI95_L2J19xL3D1aEbffB-35YYpp3L_jxs55rgUevVMzNQWToylR8w5lbpT47QRGvWmBRSMUmupYEHPaafF4BDcCnpC4wdy2k7nUVsLZng4rycPJqANHq8GLeBo_Lh646MFnPyQ3DGotQKt1dXAaSW6KLKoz8Go6RKFURQS13biBzGVQr0Txfw-sE6-bkN2D-ZnF-d_AmYBc6xf2h6JgPm4JGDO1WMWMP_2uyRs-S33yqncZfncVmpdMuUs-VVlSDFSo8JyS4GpbbJzbYn60Fx4vlLOqY9WGHXfMOUfDP6jw93BdwAAAP__qKmJoQ) but behind 2018. That year was the last time Tennessee had an open governor's race, as it does now. Voters will choose a new governor, a U.S. senator, and members of Congress. They'll also decide [three constitutional amendments](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJykkD2uqzAQhVcDHcgeDIbCxWvo8tpbook9JJbMGOEJUXZ_RbZwyyN9On8_t-WGMUV-_MeNnMi6ML1LIhE6FomCXFZMKXI-6ZC4ERr1oQUUDI3WjYIFvcSTFoN1cHfQExpfk9N26gZtLZj66fQwdv1Idw8jqqmfzODBekLynQqT1XV0l6HWCrRWo4H2TtQrsqi7YNTUr5VRFKLko5UnCTFTKURr-ly1Wp-3OrmnyF6q7l8FcwVzyaUVbh_5rGCmRF5i5lLBjMz5xZ42Yrn0d8p-5D0XCo3PXCTK66IxNbgRhy9ZHy7s75hSLIOtjHpsGNM3Wf542-ngNwAA___ST4PP), including limits on bail, a ban on a state property tax, and expanded rights for crime victims. Experts told WSMV the early numbers are a [signal, not a forecast](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJykkDHOozAQRk9jOkfjwYRQuNiGLttuiSZmSCwZG9kDKLdfscVe4O-e9ElPT9-f5_SkEEN6_6aVncgyJT5rZBEukwShVBeKMaR8cJGwMln48oSAd22MBpzISzh4stTM7oVmIOsbdqYf2rvpe7TNx9m7bx_dawCAbngsYHvoEF6mn7seWt82wV1CYwCNgYfF24u5A-7JtLOFoVuUBZ6D5HKTDwunxLUyL_F7Zd18XpvoPiJbVe0vhaPC8TzP21nX4xoVjpdf4WjgYlQ4MpX41UeWkN4677KR56oRELUUCvFi89CJT-1zeheuNeREUa-06cL1QxtXLXtJeRe9BS97Yf0_TeHYFDdvZ4gx1HuvLLxXCvFfq_zw6MPh3wAAAP__3IeR7Q).
## Titans Push Bengals to Overtime
Three days after [trading All-Pro Jeffery Simmons](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJyk0L1urDAQhuGrMZ2RPXj5KVychm5PmxLN4jE4MmZlj0DcfUQi5QbSTfXone_jOT0xxJCW_7iRZfZTorNEYqY8cWBMxWOMIe0HZQ4boVEXTaCglVpLBRPOHA6aDFbOvkAPaOaKrO6GptVdB6Zabe-96b0Dci3o3jU9-n7uCB090JOBKtgb1FqB1qo3UL-IHoo61I0zanh4YRS5wHuueSWmlKgUIh-vO6ue962KdmV-F9H8EzAKGM_zrM8jcs2HgPHmBYxa3fcgYPw15M-TkjO6kBaJMcp33uUneU_5kiVs256KnNcw47LLF2EuAsYqW_c-Q4yhtJ0watkwxO8S_uOMh4WvAAAA__8Pdog5), the heavy-underdog Titans built a 13-point lead at Cincinnati before falling 43-36 in overtime Sunday. Cam Ward threw for 304 yards and two touchdowns in his [first 300-yard game](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJyk0LFuhDAMBuCnCVtQ4oTkGDJ0YbuuHVEAc1gK4UQs0L19RU_tC3S1ftn-_q97f4-UKD8-44qBee4zniUhM-49E8dc5pgS5e3AnWnFaNULe1DgpNZSQR9HpgN7G6spDKDbaMcKg_atcdp7sNUSbmgjjn5qAcytaebRwewHdKqFwTjvKwrXQq0VaK1uFuoBsVHoozaTVW0zC6twIt72mhdkzBlLQZzT63qrHre1SmFhfhZhPgR0ArrzPOu_4Bty5QR0F1BA957JSyetkcZJ3iQvKAfMj5iKpCx_0dUepudJKVFxXlj1WCOln7P8z86OAN8BAAD__yIqgfg), and safety Amani Hooker intercepted Joe Burrow three times. Ward's 15-yard touchdown pass to Wan'Dale Robinson put Tennessee up 36-29 with 3:46 left, but Burrow answered with a tying score to Tee Higgins with 1:17 to go. Burrow, who threw for 462 yards and five touchdowns, [ran in the winner](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJykkL2upDAMhZ8GOo8SEwgUKbahu9tuiTKJmbEUEkR8Gd23XzH78wK3s2zr6Dvfr4_lw3Pi_PjpN3Ii65LpVROJ0LEIi8919SlxLicdwht5o75oQYUDaA0KFx-ET1qMb6O7o568CS05badu0NaiaZ8uRqMNDlZpqzplhxWnXk1x7MbQ92NYW3ZXoNYKtVajwdudqFdkve6iUVO_NkZRZCnHTZ4klDPVSrSmrwvrFsrWJvcU2WvT_WhwbnBOJfik8bo1ONe9HFIbnO-UHz5d07scB3hxhr9b2D9TgvIpEA-_eeEApoNugH_l389bOQmkQA8IgXPgnL0w_JEF_-Egr6k9XNxfnBLXwTZGPTbP6Y0r33R9OvwdAAD__3HjlRs) in overtime. The Titans fell to 1-7, and Cincinnati improved to 5-2.
## Memphis Boy Gives Up Birthday Gifts
A Memphis 8-year-old [spent his birthday](https://email.editor.thetennesseeflyover.com/c/eJykkb3OpDAMRZ8GOqPEhBAKim3ovm23RCGYwVL4EfHA8PYrRvsGW9vn6h7dPz_9j-fI6-u3X6gVmfqVrhRJhI5eWPyaJh8jr9tJh_BC3qibelRoQWtQ2PsgfFJvfD62A-rGm5BTq-umtLqu0eRzi3oISNooGoOuVemqwVZauco1U2PNkHP7BGqtUGvlDBYDUaWo9rocjWqqKXtYlu0oZCahdaWUiKZ4P7WKsC15bGeRPWXlrwy7DLvruopp--hyoWWfOT1PGXaPXYbd9wL0CfGd-CRguPwqIDMtIBtMRBFmv-83_MPBwU3-gC2O8OKTErx3GPiQefR3hp0_hEOk3k2lccGW4LytwGjjYHB1A4OiRgUkZy0WsywxP9pxvzhGTrbOjHotnuPXRP5zhrPFvwEAAP__2ACbkQ) handing out warm meals and bottled water to people experiencing homelessness downtown instead of opening presents. Kentintton McNeil, a Downtown Elementary student, served chicken tacos to nearly three dozen people, up from seven at his first giveaway last year. _" I want them to feel joyful about their food, and I want them to have a great night today,"_ he said. * * *
# Guest Opinion: Representatives, Not Leaders
**By Dani Pajak**
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b91e204c-fab7-4c26-9cc3-b67683aaf359?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
The other day I came across a social media post from **[Eric Synenberg](https://substack.com/redirect/5095e2a4-d05a-4644-afde-97ba9e0dcc10?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**. He was pictured alongside **[Sherrod Brown](https://substack.com/redirect/98efd0a2-a94e-4ae8-9adf-8d62baad056a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** and **Scott DiMauro** , and in the post he referred to them as leaders.
That one word stuck with me. Not because I dislike any of those individuals. Not because I oppose everything they stand for. It stuck with me because it highlighted something I've been noticing for years, especially in Ohio politics.
Too many elected officials today see themselves as leaders first and representatives second. That may sound like a small distinction, but in a representative democracy, it's the difference between serving the public and directing it.
The more I thought about it, the more I realized this mindset may explain why so many people feel disconnected from government. Whether we're talking about city councils, county government, the Statehouse, or Washington, more and more officials seem to view themselves as leaders with followers rather than representatives with constituents.
That's a dangerous shift. Because in a representative democracy, the people are supposed to lead. The elected officials are supposed to follow.
* * *
## What We Actually Elect
When someone runs for office, they aren't applying to rule. They're applying to represent. The title itself tells us what the job is supposed to be: represent us, listen to us, advocate for us, and vote on our behalf.
That's the deal. We lend elected officials our authority for a limited time. We don't surrender it permanently. Their power comes from us.
Too often, however, politicians begin acting as though the relationship works in reverse. Citizens are expected to support their agenda instead of the agenda reflecting the wishes of the citizens. That's where trust starts to break down.
* * *
## The Difference Between Representation and Leadership
A representative asks, "What do the people want?" A leader asks, "How do I get people to follow me?"
A representative understands they work for the voters. A leader can begin to believe voters should trust their judgment instead.
That distinction is more important than most people realize, because once politicians begin seeing themselves primarily as leaders, it becomes easier to justify ignoring the public when the public disagrees.
And we've all seen that happen.
* * *
## Ohio Citizens Know the Routine
Residents attend meetings, send emails, sign petitions, testify at hearings, organize their neighbors, and vote. They participate in the process exactly as they're told they should.
Then too often they hear the same response: "We hear your concerns." "We value community feedback." "We appreciate public participation."
Followed by: "We've decided to move forward anyway."
At some point, people stop believing they're being heard. And honestly, can you blame them? If residents speak, vote, and participate only to be ignored, eventually many stop engaging altogether.
That's not healthy for democracy.
* * *
## The Euclid Example
I don't have to look very far for an example. I live in Euclid.
Residents voted against joining RITA. The issue went before the voters, and the voters rejected it. In my view, that should have settled the matter. Instead, city officials ultimately moved forward despite the result.
Whether you support RITA or oppose it isn't the point. The point is that voters spoke, and government decided it knew better. To me, that wasn't representation. It was leadership. It was elected officials deciding that their judgment outweighed the decision made by the people they were elected to serve.
Two council members associated with that era of Euclid politics have since pursued higher office. Maria Jukic, a former Euclid council member, is now running for Congress. Christine McIntosh, also a former Euclid council member, is running for Cuyahoga County Council.
This is not about attacking either individual. It's about asking a simple question: If voters explicitly say no, and elected officials find a way around that decision anyway, who is actually being represented?
Because it isn't the people who cast those votes.
* * *
## Who Gets Heard?
Every voter should ask themselves a simple question: When an elected official makes a decision, who are they really listening to? The residents? Or the donors, lobbyists, party organizations, consultants, and special interests with greater access and influence?
Most ordinary citizens have very little influence compared with organizations that have money, connections, and full-time political advocates.
A resident gets three minutes at a microphone. A special interest group gets a private meeting. A resident sends an email. A PAC writes a check.
That's not how representative government is supposed to function.
Government should be most responsive to the people who live with the consequences of its decisions. Instead, too often it appears more responsive to those with the greatest resources and access.
That perception, whether fair or unfair, is fueling public frustration across Ohio.
* * *
## The Rise of the Political Class
Part of the problem is that politics has become a career path. People move from one office to another, building networks, fundraising operations, and political alliances along the way. Eventually many become surrounded almost entirely by other political insiders.
The farther someone gets from everyday voters, the easier it becomes to believe they know better than the public they're supposed to serve.
That's when representatives begin to see themselves as leaders. And once that happens, the public becomes something to manage rather than something to represent.
* * *
## Humility Is the Missing Ingredient
Good representation requires humility. It requires recognizing that holding public office doesn't make someone wiser than the people who elected them. It requires accepting that citizens will sometimes disagree. It requires respecting those disagreements even when they're inconvenient.
Most importantly, it requires remembering that the power belongs to the people.
Every council seat belongs to the people. Every county office belongs to the people. Every legislative district belongs to the people. Every congressional seat belongs to the people.
The politician is just renting it for a while. Too many have forgotten that.
* * *
## Ohio Doesn't Need More Leaders
Frankly, Ohio doesn't suffer from a shortage of leaders. Every campaign promises leadership. Every consultant sells leadership. Every elected official celebrates leadership.
What we don't have enough of is representation.
We need city council members who respect the will of their residents. We need county officials who remember who hired them. We need state legislators who spend more time listening than lecturing. We need members of Congress who remember they are public servants, not public managers.
Most importantly, we need elected officials who stop calling themselves leaders long enough to remember what they were elected to be.
Representatives.
Because representatives don't ask people to follow them. They follow the people.
And if citizens have grown cynical about government, perhaps the problem isn't the public. Perhaps it's that too many elected officials have forgotten who they're supposed to represent.
Ohio doesn't need more leaders.
It needs more representatives.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/f460b8a2-adb3-48b4-9caa-c2944c077475?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|

## Editor's Response: We Need Actual Leadership
**By Matt Diemer**
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/7c2d1ca6-264d-4646-9461-c16ce63573d2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
I understand where Dani is coming from. "Representatives, not leaders" is a good slogan. It's populist, and it speaks to something everybody wants in a democracy: to know that their voice matters.
People want somebody who goes to Congress, the Statehouse, or the governor's office to act on their behalf. They want to be heard and taken seriously. And they are tired of a political class that congratulates itself while treating the public as an inconvenience.
The way political insiders talk about one another's "leadership," as though every person holding a microphone is George Washington crossing the Delaware, is cringeworthy. The self-congratulation and navel-gazing deserve an eye roll.
But I reach the opposite conclusion from Dani.
Right now, I don't think representation is what we're missing most. We need actual, bold leadership. And real leadership has real consequences.
* * *
### Courage Requires Something to Lose
During my first campaign, I read _Profiles in Courage_ , written by a young senator named John F. Kennedy.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/dadfe3c6-050b-4b47-b7ea-9242a7e7c8a4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
What stayed with me was the idea of courage in the face of consequences. Political destruction. Financial loss. A career ending. Relationships breaking down.
The ideals took precedence. They were important enough that risking something substantial became necessary.
That is a very different thing from finding the position that will make the largest number of people happy with you.
Right now, I see too many people trying to get in line, convinced that fitting into the existing political structure is the only way forward. Being agreeable, building the right relationships, and becoming everybody's best buddy get treated as qualifications for office.
But serious crises and complex problems require something much rarer.
They require somebody willing to make a decision, explain it, and accept the consequences of following it through.
* * *
### What I Mean by Leadership
Before going further, I should define the word as I'm using it.
Leadership is having a vision, the conviction to pursue it, and the ability to communicate it well enough to build a coalition capable of achieving it.
The vision alone is insufficient. You have to develop a plan, bring people together, and execute it.
Only after that work has been done can we fully judge, in hindsight, whether the direction was correct. Leadership involves accepting that uncertainty and taking responsibility for the result.
That is why I disagree with the idea that an elected official's central question should simply be, "What do the people want?"
In my view, representation framed entirely that way becomes populism. Find the majority position, adopt it, and follow the votes. If the majority already agrees with you, the political decision is easy. You have the people, you have the votes, and you have a path to winning.
Where is the courage required in that?
And is the most popular decision always the best decision?
Dani describes a representative who listens to the public and a leader who asks people to follow. But bringing people toward a vision requires more than demanding their trust. It requires explaining where you want to go, why you believe it is right, and what it will take to get there.
People then have something to evaluate beyond whether you have repeated their current preferences back to them.
* * *
### What Happens When the Popular Becomes Unpopular?
The harder test comes after an election.
You win a majority behind an idea. You begin carrying it out. Then the transition becomes difficult.
The popular thing becomes unpopular. The inexpensive thing becomes costly. The changes people supported in principle become difficult in practice.
What happens then?
Do you abandon the vision because the public mood has shifted? Do you move to whatever position now has the easiest majority? Or do you have the clarity and conviction to explain the difficulty, keep the coalition together, and carry the work through?
Following a vision through turmoil takes courage. It takes the ability to communicate with people who are frustrated, uncertain, or beginning to lose faith in what they supported.
That, to me, is leadership.
The responsibility is to help bring people somewhere that will benefit the greatest number of them, even when getting there is strained and turbulent.
And the sacrifice required may be your own popularity, your position, or your political future.
That is a cost I want somebody seeking office to understand before asking for the job.
* * *
### The People Calling Themselves Leaders Often Aren't
Dani is right about the misuse of the title. Most of the people celebrating one another as leaders have done very little to earn it.
To be perfectly honest, some of them are not doing a particularly good job of representing people, either.
But their failure does not persuade me that we have too much leadership. It persuades me that we have too many people claiming the title without accepting the responsibility or the risk that comes with it.
I want people with convictions strong enough to withstand a difficult period. People who can build a coalition around a clear vision and keep working when the applause stops. People willing to risk their own careers for an outcome they believe will serve the public.
That is what I took from _Profiles in Courage_. And that is what I think we are missing.
Dani wants elected officials who remember whom they serve. I want people who can do that and still have the courage to set a direction, bring others along, and see it through.
We need the person willing to fall on the knife and, in hindsight, look at the scar and say it was worth it.

A representative understands they work for the voters. A leader can begin to believe voters should trust their judgment instead. In my view, that should have settled the matter. Instead, city officials ultimately moved forward despite the result. Whether you support RITA or oppose it isn't the point. The point is that voters spoke, and government decided it knew better. To me, that wasn't representation. It was leadership. It was elected officials deciding that their judgment outweighed the decision made by the people they were elected to serve. It's about asking a simple question: If voters explicitly say no, and elected officials find a way around that decision anyway, who is actually being represented? Because it isn't the people who cast those votes. Who Gets Heard? Every voter should ask themselves a simple question: When an elected official makes a decision, who are they really listening to? A special interest group gets a private meeting. A resident sends an email. A PAC writes a check. That's not how representative government is supposed to function. Government should be most responsive to the people who live with the consequences of its decisions. Instead, too often it appears more responsive to those with the greatest resources and access. We need members of Congress who remember they are public servants, not public managers. Most importantly, we need elected officials who stop calling themselves leaders long enough to remember what they were elected to be. Representatives. Because representatives don't ask people to follow them. They follow the people. And if citizens have grown cynical about government, perhaps the problem isn't the public. Hey everyone,
Early voting has ended in Ohio. Now, we leave it all on the field.
**Ohio -- I am ready to win and give our families a voice in the Senate once again.**
But hundreds of thousands of Ohioans are still considering who to vote for, or whether to vote at all. Today, our team is doing whatever it takes to reach these folks and earn their support.
So I have a request for you:
If you've already voted or made your plan, the most meaningful action you can take is donating to help our team. If that's too much to ask, the next best thing is joining us by volunteering a few hours of your time to help us get out the vote.
[Donate](https://substack.com/redirect/fa80641e-a2f5-4a56-9234-ed9f9e71a70b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
[Volunteer](https://substack.com/redirect/e95ae393-2d61-45ac-8804-10c94b78336f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
**We 're ending this campaign the way we've run it: together.**
Together, we are making history in Ohio. A handful of corrupt billionaires think they can buy power and keep this rigged system working in their favor. We're proving that our voice is louder than their money. Ohio belongs to us, not Peter Thiel, Elon Musk, the crypto crowd, or Donald Trump.
More than 430,000 people have contributed to this campaign. Thousands and thousands have stepped up to knock doors, register voters, and make phone calls. And so far, over 1.6 million Ohioans have voted.
I need your help to finish the job. We need to get our message out to as many voters as possible and make sure they have a plan to cast their ballots tomorrow.
I want all of us to be confident that we did all we could to win this race - and pave a path to retaking the Senate too. We can't take anything for granted.
I wish I was done asking, but **[one of the most meaningful steps you can take today to increase our odds of victory tomorrow is making a grassroots donation to fund our final push](https://substack.com/redirect/fa80641e-a2f5-4a56-9234-ed9f9e71a70b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**. We're staring down a $75K cut to our mobilization plan today. Hundreds of supporters have stepped up since Patrick reached out last night, and I'm hoping one last push will get us there.
If you've already given, thank you for getting us to this point. If you've forwarded these notes, talked to your family or friends or coworkers, shown up to a rally, or volunteered to talk to voters or write postcards, that means so much to me as well.
None of us want to look back on this final stretch with regrets. I'm so proud of this team. Thanks for standing with me.
Sherrod Brown

name: America First War Room Sponsor
subject: Your IRA & 401(k) isn't on the ballot...
body:
Prices rose half a percent in September alone. Whoever wins tomorrow,
that number stays.

View in Web Browser
[https://link.email.america1stwarroom.com/click/e949207/UaHR0cHM6Ly93cm8ubnVjbGV1c2VtYWlsLmNvbS9hbXBsaWZ5L3YvOHFiM0hiVkhKdg/SZW1haWxfYW1lcmljYU9ORXN0d2Fycm9vbV9jb20yNjExMDI/LbmNsWWxxU2o2Qg/qP2hpZHM9bmNMRVlJYUI3Zmw2cHlsc10/gauhyPg/s0q5861aa04

YOUR IRA & 401(K) ISN'T ON THE BALLOT

Tomorrow you help pick who goes to (or stays in) Washington. One thing
isn't on your ballot: what your money buys.

Government figures out Thursday show prices rose half a percent in
September alone, and 3.6% over the past year.

When prices climb, the dollars in your savings buy a little less food,
a little less at the pharmacy, a little less of everything you live
on.

[Two grocery bags with prescription bottles on a kitchen table. A
label reading $100 in 2016 points to the left bag, full of bread,
apples, bananas and greens, with three pill bottles in front. A red
label reading Same $100 today: about $72 worth points to the right
bag, which holds much less, with two pill bottles. Caption: Your $100
from 2016 now buys about $72 worth.] [https://link.email.america1stwarroom.com/click/e949207/UaHR0cHM6Ly9saW5rLmdvbGRjby5jb20vNTVwXQ/SZW1haWxfYW1lcmljYU9ORXN0d2Fycm9vbV9jb20yNjExMDI/LbmNsWWxxU2o2Qg/gauhyPg/s9n6cab135c

Even Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said last week that when Americans look
around,

_"...THEY SEE THE PRICES ARE UP."_
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh

If you're retired, no boss hands you a raise to catch up. Your savings
just have to stretch further.

You can't vote on prices. But you can decide how your savings are
spread out [https://link.email.america1stwarroom.com/click/e949207/UaHR0cHM6Ly9saW5rLmdvbGRjby5jb20vNTVwXS4/SZW1haWxfYW1lcmljYU9ORXN0d2Fycm9vbV9jb20yNjExMDI/LbmNsWWxxU2o2Qg/gauhyPg/s8i01a80453

That's why savers near or in retirement can diversify part of their
savings into physical gold and silver.

From 1973 to 1979, when prices rose about 9% a year, gold rose about
35% a year. Silver soared too.

[Bar chart of average yearly rise from 1973 to 1979: prices rose
8.8% a year, gold rose 35% a year. Past performance is not a promise
of future results.] [https://link.email.america1stwarroom.com/click/e949207/UaHR0cHM6Ly9saW5rLmdvbGRjby5jb20vNTVwXQ/SZW1haWxfYW1lcmljYU9ORXN0d2Fycm9vbV9jb20yNjExMDI/LbmNsWWxxU2o2Qg/gauhyPg/s9n6cab135c

That's history, not a promise. Gold and silver have rough stretches
too, be very wary of anyone who says otherwise.

## Team Turner is Working Hard and Running Through the Finish Line
---
Friends,Tomorrow is Election Day.There is too much at risk to sit at home and not get out and vote Mike Turner for Congress.Team Turner has been out working hard, delivering results, and fighting for every vote.Read on and learn more about what we've been up to in October!

---

We have never been closer to getting this across the finish line.You can watch my full remarks below and learn more about our efforts to restore the pensions of the Delphi Salaried Retirees [here.](https://click-493811.icptrack.com/icp/relay.php?r=126057447&msgid=1044827&act=NE1B&c=493811&pid=12638209&destination=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.daytondailynews.com%2Flocal%2Ftrump-meets-with-delphi-retirees-at-vandalia-rally-event%2Farticle_8d2c2b64-ea28-5547-ac5e-c55b96662f8c.html&cf=64880&v=3a681ac14a6605f594ead8cc7df650f7186d17eb29fd102bef04d6b42884fb1c)

Throughout the month of October, I have been working hard knocking doors throughout the district. We have knocked doors in every county in the district, including the communities of Dayton, Miamisburg, Clayton, Oakwood, Middletown, Xenia, Englewood, and others. We had some great conversations with voters about the important issues facing our community, the successes we've had, and the work left to do. We are thankful for the support we're seeing across the district!

# Monday, November 2, 2026
---|---
**Good Morning!** On this day in 1920, Pittsburgh's KDKA made the first commercial radio broadcast in America, reading the Harding-Cox presidential election returns from a shack on the roof of a Westinghouse plant to about a thousand listeners within 500 miles. [Hear a recreation of that first broadcast here](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkL2OpDAQhJ8GMpDdZswQOLiEbC69EPmnDT1j8MjuG7Rvv2JfYdMqqT7V9--xPCwlOta_dkfDMS8HnjUhM5Ylplwo2CeyL7ZuK5bdHoUyLyBAd1J2AhbrmT64yDaYiAioWjRynJSWkwDdbkYPbhT36JzWo7LCDtOEMTqQYdJ6uOmWzDUnpQAplYBbryavYAgaxR0giLEZBAbiXPpnpoM3jOkrf7D0Pu9tMhvzuzbqTwNzA_N5nr139bpx9Q3Mb2Ku7n9ZtwbmK29gfoWXrd1GlXMh37mSbfC2cltMeJ-UElV9cdfdUvrh8O_sfAx8BwAA__8EVHp1). Take a second look at those crumpled lottery tickets in your wallet. A Michigan man carried a $1 million Powerball winner [around for two months](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLGOtCAQgJ8GOwwM6kpB8TdU_-6VVxqUUdmgGJxbsm9_8e4RrpnmS2a-bz7vw92FGPbl4TY0NKdhx3JGJMI8zDHl4N0TacruXBfMm9tzSDSAgI5LyQUMbqLwwkFW3syIgKpCI29adVIL6KrVKC80NiPO4-Q1ONdoqZpejW2re4U3XQVzrZNSgJRKQFsrPSlofIeiB_DixhqBPlDK9TOFnVac4zu9MNdT2qpoVqLjZOofA8vAllLqryNcjIH98H54YDkZ2OsIAysFA6uuERNR4vcwrWFxO_-frug3P1LBPLoYOZXEt7TTevL4CxnYtoUrT_USWmBgq2z8UUKM4ewu02VzIf6Y0d_--TLwHQAA___43odQ) and only found out when he came up short for a soda. We have the whole story in _Et Cetera_. Have you ever won anything on a lottery ticket? Hit reply and tell us, even if it was five bucks. The clocks fell back this weekend, and almost nobody is happy about it. But ending the time change is harder than it sounds. America tried going without it once, and what happened that winter turned the whole country around in a matter of weeks. Fifty years later, the fight is back on, so how did we end up changing our clocks in the first place, and is this the year it finally stops? On today's episode of _Flyover Focus_ , we dig into the strange history of Daylight Saving Time, the 1974 experiment that changed everything, and the three ways this could all end. [Tune in here!](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykz0FuqzAQgOHT4F2QZwwGFl486YldqrabLC3HHoIjgyMzIeL2VXqFHuD_pP9ytmcXU1xvH24hw1O2K722RMxU7JRyicHdiX1x23yjsri1xMwWJeoTwEmidZ7jThZEMBMRkhJkoBuUhkGiFrMJWiro--s0AAYVuqH1XQP62snet33jRDRvDkAigJLY1mrwCpugSfaIQXZVIylEzqW-57jyTFM68k6l9nkRyczMj61S_yocKxyP_ORnfaUKx8_L8dXa8f939qKY8HjFlOKm395tcTH99vy3693gTwAAAP__LKBqRw) Today's sponsor, [Granola](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykz7FugzAQxvGnwVuQfQYTBg9d2NK1o3XFZ7jI4MiciPr2Vaq-Qfbv-0n_r1u4IWfel0_cyEsqYafnkUmEaki5VI54J5krHutCdcO9cpEAGtzFmIuGgLPwScGo6BMRkFXkzTBaZ0YNTq3-2g-DtX2nR-jibKIzzrnvwWKfUq9RK_YvzhgNxlgNfWvH2UIXHekrQNRD02mKLKW298K7rJTyTzmptnPZVParyKOxHw1MDUxLaZeKe8nYIjcw_U9V9fHx5Jz5cC9v2ZDz31_eqz49_AYAAP__Ivtqkg), turns your meetings into clear notes, saves shared slides as Snapshots, and helps you find what was agreed upon. ## Jet Crash Kills 9 in Florida
A Learjet carrying nine people [plunged into a mobile home park](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0LGK4zAQxvGnkTsFaeTIp0LFweEu1yzLlmYkjWMF2QrykJC3Xxz2DbYeGP6_7-syXTCXvF3_40qe5zpt9NwLMVOb5lJbTngjjg335Uptxa3lyhMosFJrqWDCyPlBk-6Sn4mATEdeD85Y7RTYbvHOUOwp9GHWBlPSFghNIKuCdbaHocv-eKe1Aq2NgvPJuGigT5bUH4CkBtErSplrO91q3nihubzqg9op1rUrfmG-78L8FTAKGDHEg3DcBIyfHwLGQthuxNJJDBVbkm8O7fKOZZWBMC7yxypnRAHjzrW9hBlzEuafNsNwNmfnuubT_ZlLybs9oq4r5vKO4N9N9_DwHQAA__9lo4Hl) in Greenacres, Florida, west of Palm Beach, around 12:50 p.m. ET Sunday. No one on board survived. Dear Neighbor, Before you cast your vote, I invite you to watch my debate on News 8 and hear my proposals to address rising costs, hold utility executives accountable, and make it easier for people to work without losing the benefits they depend on.
## Keep the Lights Local
Hear me discuss the **Keep the Lights Local Act** and why our utility system should put the needs of our community first.
## No Bonuses for Utility Executives
Families struggling with utility bills deserve accountability. Watch me explain my support of legistlation that would stop bonuses for utility executives.
## Address the Benefits Cliff
Earning more should help families move forward. Yet the **benefits cliff** can cause someone to lose essential assistance when their income crosses an eligibility threshold—even when the increase in pay does not cover what they lose. I propose a **sliding scale that allows benefits to decrease gradually as earned income rises, with a buy-in option to maintain coverage.** The goal is to make healthcare more affordable and help more people enter the workforce, take on additional hours, or accept a raise without putting their family’s stability at risk. **You deserve to hear the candidates discuss the issues that affect your daily life. Watch the debate and decide for yourself.**

The clocks fell back this weekend, and almost nobody is happy about it. But ending the time change is harder than it sounds. America tried going without it once, and what happened that winter turned the whole country around in a matter of weeks. ## Deep Ellum Shootings Leave 4 Dead
Three shootings in Dallas' Deep Ellum entertainment district [left four people dead](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJyk0DuOrDAQheHVmMwtV9m8Agc3IeubTogKXGCPDEbY_WD3o54tTHyko0__1328U4hhX__Txra8lzTu_MqRS-Fz5MhzCWl3dOWSzi17nvIj-zCiwkYCSIUjzSU8eYTK2Um5Hiq20Pa6QdUrqLwFPdVqNgDcGZw617a1blRN2tQaTLdUwX7eABQCKtD9bV7YmK5h6k3Xa9LCKHahpPNWPBd-U17ilZ583ua0VdH6Uo4s9D-Bg8CBphn0ZxE4fNSXwOFIMcwsM13SSMfkJNQy7N-Pk53MfNBJhWX2KZWwr1k6ipGy9BRjejHvcg-rLwIHVErVvUKBQ3Vad7xCjCE3rTBq3SjEX1H5Y8inxZ8AAAD__3yBhy8) and about 15 wounded in the early hours after Halloween night. Police are still working to learn whether they were connected. The [first call came in](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkLHOozAQhJ_GdCDv4jO4cHEN3X_tlWixl2BpwRF2QvL2p-QVrp7RaL7v78_8Q0nScftDO_v6WvN88FWEa-VzZuFQUz4ivUvN5142XsqjbGlGjbYFaDXOFGp68gxN9IuODhr2MLjeonYams0DxcXZX-MIMBjLIy0DLD2GEHqrkZcm-c8agEZADb3rwsrGjJbJmdH11CujOaaaz65uXPlFZZV3fvLZhbw34rda70X1vxVOCqfrurpjCXG9PrHC6QOkcJIcSBROkUSotBuJ5Iv5aMuWc03HrbSR-d6yyGNvV6rfttHOgTUKp-b08X4lkVTsoIy-7ZTk-6D-p7inx38BAAD__672gzI) about 12:19 a.m. from the 2600 block of Elm Street. Gunfire broke out just after 1 a.m. a block south on Main Street, then a third time around 1:35 a.m. on South Crowdus Street. Police said [five people were shot](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkL2yozAMhZ_GdGYs4QVcuNiGLttuyRgsgmcEzmAlJG9_h7zCbaU5P9_5fxtvIXHa7__CRl7eSx53OguTCB0jMc2S8h7Dp0g-trLSVJ5lTSMabDWANjiGWdKLRqiin0x0UJGHzjUtGmegWr2h3iKEBaGbl95ShKm1vbOBWqDuz1Qlf7kBGAQ00Lh6XsjavqXgbO-a0ChrKCbJRy0rCb1DWfiTX3TUc94q9qvIo6jmr8JB4XCeZz1P5cK4_gqHr0ThcJ0UDpFC5I-ORA9NzM9NlzVnSfu96BiYQ7nIQF-tFA7V4ePjTMyptJ2y5r6FxN9k-eVgL48_AQAA__-UOYAu) during an apparent altercation in a convenience store parking lot at the first scene. Officers two blocks away responded quickly. Three people died at the second shooting and one at the third. Police Chief Daniel Comeaux said the department was fully staffed for Halloween, made some arrests, and is [searching for more suspects](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkLGOhCAURb8GOwwgg1JQbGM3225pEJ4DyVMm8kZn_n7j_sI2t7q5N-f83Ke7z5i3x7dfwdF7KdMGZ0Uggn0ChEC5bNF_KpV9rQnm-qopT0oow6XkQk0-UD5gkk10s4hWNuBkbzujhBWySc4OQlhxkz7MaghgfK8lLMHoIPvhNndNdtealEJJJWRn27CA1oMBb_VgO98xLSBmKntLCQjevi74KQfsbShrgy4RPSvrvpgamRrP82yX8lYmlVelsl0lpsYLi6kxAjw5IL5WnjxiOQE2XlMplLdH5Qj-gCsrcc0j-NjsLj7PjJir6ZkWj9Vn_Dumf_o6nPoNAAD__8EagdA). "_This is completely unacceptable for it to take place in Dallas_ ," he said.
## Cold Front and Election Day Storms
A cold front will sweep a line of storms across Texas from tonight into Election Day Tuesday, then usher in cooler, drier air, with some areas seeing [lows in the 40s](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkLFuwyAURb8Gb1jwcOwwMHTxlq4dLQKPgIqNBa9x8vdVov5Bx6t7da50vi7LxaacttunXdHQI5Rlw6NlJMK6YEZHqWzePhuVuraI1_bTYlpAwMil5AIW6yjdcZGdN1fhtezQyEmrEYQWsovGah8kBj85mOQYTi4odToDBI1q8gK7ZF40KQVIEFLp3gUchvOIVg9nraxig0CfqNSeIhI-bAv5We5Ye1fWLptItDemPhjMDObjOHoXa9le7SujpYiVwWwrJZeRwfyG8APxGzfP_xY82FrQ2Ubclew5wElIJXS_x72rxu9Hyjm1cWKDuK025fc9_dPa3cBvAAAA___xFIM7). Dallas-Fort Worth faces a slight risk of severe weather (level 2 out of 5) overnight, with possible hail, localized flooding, damaging winds, [and brief tornadoes](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkLGOozAQhp8GOiPbcBAXLq5Jl2uvRINnHFsyOLInkLz9iuy-wbafRp_m-__f5hvEFLf7P1jJ8svneaOjJmKmMlMixzFvCO_Kuaw10FKfNcRZSz0KpYTUMziOO82qRbtINKolqybTj1oaqdpg5US9Mk5qnMyCPSG65Y83YMBokIBttKdNKamVlqo3nfM0DJeRwAwX00PfDJIwci4dB2J6QfXpnXcqnctrm2xgftSm_9voa6Ovx3F0Pr-Gs-M8OBEBByqNviKkBFX8AIG0VRI-30UNJT-xio9eQCBAUWmnQuI7XbicUPiSN26LxccRU4p1nJpB3leI6fML_3LC3eqvAAAA__8JnIp3). Storms should taper off early Tuesday, leaving clearing skies and highs in the low to mid-70s. Central Texas is under a level 1 out of 5 risk for hail and gusty winds, with storms crossing the I-35 corridor around 4 a.m. Tuesday. Rain should [clear out by 9 a.m.](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkL2u4yAQRp_G7sYCjGxTUGyTLttuafEzxEgYIpjE8duvknvvE9z2aDQ63_l3Xa8mpphvf82Oml6hrBmPlpAI64oJHcWSvTkblbq3DW17tC2ugokJOAcmVuMoPnHlvdeWecV71HxW4ySYYrzfNOISnPB-lM5NXFkr7Gwt44uSo2BG9lG_v3HOBBeMj2pwAaVcJjRKLmo0YycZ-kilDrQh4cu0kM7yxDq4svdJb0T31o1_OnHpxOU4jiGU12wejWJ-n7whGtqwduLyheEbgMfcEEK5wb2iQ48NPlNPcCV5CLVkAuNqaQ0cZqomwUcBLIZSEX4agTdnX7W_HzGl2Ka5k-y2m5g-kvTLtk8t_gcAAP__-6GT1w), leaving dry conditions for voters. Houston gets the front last, with the heaviest rain expected from late morning through evening Tuesday, along with strong winds and potential hail. name: Roy Cooper
subject: Thanks ahead of time
body:
I'm just grateful for you, Peter.
| [](https://act.roycooper.com/go/15912?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1757&source=&t=1&akid=5265%2E124072%2EswWOlf) | | | |
---
Peter,
I know my team and I have been emailing a _lot_ lately – so I’m just grateful that you’d take the time to read this.
That said, we’re less than 24 hours out from Election Day, and if we’re going to meet our final $1 million voter outreach goal tonight, we need to pick up the pace. [**_If everyone reading right now gives $5, we’ll be on track, so can I count on you to donate?_**](https://act.roycooper.com/go/15912?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1757&amount=5&t=8&akid=5265%2E124072%2EswWOlf)
| | [DONATE](https://act.roycooper.com/go/14264?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1757&amount=5&t=9&akid=5265%2E124072%2EswWOlf)
---
Falling short is simply not an option – and I’ll tell you why:
JD Vance joined Michael Whatley for a third North Carolina rally just last week. Plus, GOP outside spending groups have poured tens of millions into attack ads against me.
_With the latest poll showing support for Whatley on the rise, it all seems to be working._
Not only would missing our $1 million goal leave us struggling to win over the last few undecided voters left – **we’d also risk letting Whatley and the GOP have the last word as they make up their minds.**
With Senate control hinging on the outcome of this race, and the stakes for our country this high, we set goals like this in the hopes that people like you will step up when it matters most.
[**_Now is one of those times, Peter, so please: Pitch in $5 or any amount now to help us close the gap, mobilize voters across NC and flip this must-win seat._**](https://act.roycooper.com/go/15912?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1757&amount=5&t=10&akid=5265%2E124072%2EswWOlf)
_If you've saved payment information with ActBlue Express, your donation will go through immediately:_ | | | [DONATE $5](https://act.roycooper.com/go/16105?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1757&amount=5&t=11&akid=5265%2E124072%2EswWOlf)
---
| | [DONATE $25](https://act.roycooper.com/go/16105?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1757&amount=25&t=12&akid=5265%2E124072%2EswWOlf)
---
| | [DONATE $50](https://act.roycooper.com/go/16105?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1757&amount=50&t=13&akid=5265%2E124072%2EswWOlf)
---
| | [OTHER AMOUNT](https://act.roycooper.com/go/15912?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1757&t=14&akid=5265%2E124072%2EswWOlf)
---
Thank you in advance for helping us make a course correction for our country and return power in Washington to the hands of working people.
With gratitude,
Roy Cooper
| |
* * *
[](https://act.roycooper.com/go/15912?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1757&t=2&akid=5265%2E124072%2EswWOlf)
Democrat Roy Cooper is running for U.S. Senate to help take back the Majority for Democrats. North Carolina is Democrats’ best chance to flip a seat from red to blue — the path to stopping Republicans in Washington starts here.

National Republicans will target North Carolina as a key battleground and invest heavily in defeating us.

Cooper is a former state legislator, Attorney General, and most recently Governor of North Carolina. North Carolina will be the most competitive Senate election of 2026, and Cooper enters the race as the most formidable candidate of either party.

Cooper’s signature achievements include helping to expand Medicaid and helping make NC the top state for business by creating thousands of jobs and growing the clean energy economy.

[**_Donate today to help win this seat and flip the Senate blue._**](https://act.roycooper.com/go/15912?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1757&source=&t=3&akid=5265%2E124072%2EswWOlf)
| | [DONATE](https://act.roycooper.com/go/15912?refcode=email_fr_pros_jtk1757&source=&t=4&akid=5265%2E124072%2EswWOlf)

It's been an incredible journey since we launched our campaign 18 months ago, and now everything we've worked toward is within reach.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/a8f416d3-1465-4c3b-bf75-db2e2ee7760b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|

Tomorrow the polls will close, the votes will be tallied, and we'll learn who New Hampshire's next Senator will be.
**[If you're already on board and ready to help us flip the Senate, can I count on you to rush a $15 contribution right now?](https://substack.com/redirect/a8f416d3-1465-4c3b-bf75-db2e2ee7760b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
[DONATE](https://substack.com/redirect/a8f416d3-1465-4c3b-bf75-db2e2ee7760b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
This is our _**final**_ chance to build the resources we need to stay competitive with the MAGA billionaires and national Republican groups propping up John Sununu's campaign.
**This is the culmination of everything we have built together -- a movement of people who believe in a freer, fairer future. **
**[We set a goal to raise $300,000 to our Last Chance Fund to ensure we reach every single New Hampshire voter and make their voices heard. Can you chip in $15 before it's too late?](https://substack.com/redirect/a8f416d3-1465-4c3b-bf75-db2e2ee7760b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
[DONATE](https://substack.com/redirect/a8f416d3-1465-4c3b-bf75-db2e2ee7760b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
The GOP and the MAGA billionaires backing John Sununu are determined to flip this seat red. That's why they are spending more than $67 million to try and buy this seat -- and they're counting on us falling short of our goal.
With Election Day less than 24 hours away, every minute counts now. _**And every dollar has to stretch even further in these final moments.**_
That's why I'm reaching out again to ask for your support. Not because it's a nice-to-have, but because hitting this goal is the only way we'll be able to win this race.
**[Please, will you chip in what you can to our Last Chance Fund to help us reach our $300,000 fundraising goal and keep us on track to win this race tomorrow?](https://substack.com/redirect/a8f416d3-1465-4c3b-bf75-db2e2ee7760b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**

Chris

On the October 24, 2026 edition of Fox's Ingraham Angle -- ten days before the midterms -- Laura Ingraham put the hypothetical to Mike Davis: founder and president of the Article III Project, former chief counsel for nominations to the Senate Judiciary Committee's Republicans, a clerk for Neil Gorsuch. What happens to the Second Amendment if Democrats pack the Supreme Court?
Davis needed three words: "It would be _gone_."
Then he said the rest: they would take away our God-given right to keep and bear arms, and they would claim the Second Amendment covers only the National Guard. Hyperbole? Only if you don't know the math or the history. Both cut his way.
The math behind "gone." District of Columbia v. Heller (2008) recognized an individual right to keep a handgun at home, 5-4\. The Court described the right as pre-existing -- the amendment protects a right it did not create, the same Creator-endowed logic as the Declaration -- which is why Davis says God-given. But it was close. Four dissents argued the right belongs to the militias -- the "organized militia" the federal government reorganized as the National Guard by the Militia Act of 1903 and the National Defense Act of 1916. Justice John Paul Stevens wrote that dissent, and in March 2018 he published a New York Times op-ed titled, without euphemism, "Repeal the Second Amendment." McDonald (2010) applied the right to the states, 5-4\. Bruen (2022) extended it outside the home, 6-3.
The anti-Heller bloc currently numbers three -- the Court's three Democratic appointees. Add four seats and it is seven to six. Heller, McDonald, and Bruen flip in a single term; D.C.-style handgun bans are constitutional again; the militia reading becomes the law of the land. Hillary Clinton herself once called D.C.'s ban "reasonable" -- a polite way of dissenting from Heller. That is what "gone" means: not a repeal passed by Congress and ratified by thirty-eight states, but seven justices declaring that the words mean what the dissidents always said they meant -- Guard service and a permission slip. Repealing the text is impossible. Repainting its meaning takes a majority of both chambers and a willing president.
The thirteen-circuits excuse. Days before the segment, on a podcast, Clinton supplied the justification the packing push had been missing: "You know, it used to be that you'd have one justice for each circuit. We now have 13 circuits, we should have 13 justices." Add her headline caveat -- "we should seriously look at expanding the court while the Democrats are in power" -- and note that Elizabeth Warren backs the idea, while Jim Clyburn said on Meet the Press that "we ought to expand."
Davis destroyed this in about thirty seconds, and the historical record supports every syllable. There have been nine justices since 1869. Yes, for most of the Court's first century the justices rode circuit -- and while they did, Congress did grow the bench alongside the circuits: six justices and three circuits in 1789; a seventh of each in 1807; the eighth and ninth in 1837; a tenth circuit in 1863. But in 1891 Congress created the Courts of Appeals so the justices would not have to ride, and by 1911 circuit-riding was formally abolished. The workload rationale died with it.
Then comes the proof. Congress kept adding circuits and never added a justice. The Tenth Circuit was created in 1929 -- the bench stayed at nine. The Federal Circuit in 1982 -- nine. Of today's thirteen circuits, two (the D.C. Circuit and the Federal Circuit) aren't _geographic_ circuits at all. One justice per circuit was never a constitutional rule or a statute; it was a workload arrangement from the horseback era that ended 135 years ago. Clinton was quoting an administrative convenience of 1837 as if it were a principle of 2026. The circuits are geography. The bench is not.
The question that ends the debate. If the court truly needs thirteen -- if it's arithmetic about circuits -- why is no Democrat demanding thirteen right now, with a Republican president and a Republican Senate? Because the demand follows power, not principle. The last time Democrats held the House, the Senate, and the White House with a 6-3 court, Senator Ed Markey and Representative Hank Johnson introduced the Judiciary Act of 2021: exactly four seats, a thirteen-justice court. It went nowhere -- the filibuster stood, Manchin and Sinema stood with it -- and the number quietly disappeared until this month's election-eve revival. To be fair to Clinton, "look at" and "see if we could make it work" is softer than enactment. But that is the tell. A principle doesn't wait to see if it can work; a device does. The device resurfaces only when the court's composition is the prize.
Four votes. Franklin Roosevelt wanted six extra seats in 1937 -- a court of fifteen -- and the Senate Judiciary Committee killed the plan in July, 10-8\. The modern ask is smaller and surgical: four seats turn every contested line -- Heller, Bruen, the rest of the 5-4s and 6-3s -- into seven-vote majorities overnight. Not reform. The minimum winning number.
That is Davis's real answer, and Ingraham's monologue -- which RealClearPolitics clipped under the title "The Democrats Stampede To Pack the Supreme Court" -- framed it: a court you can pack is a court you can own. Nine justices have held the text above simple majorities since 1869. The circuits figure is the fig leaf; four is the operative number; and "It would be gone" is the price of admission.

What Happens to the Second Amendment if Democrats Pack the Court? | | | Nov 2 | | | | | | | | | | | | On the October 24, 2026 edition of Fox's Ingraham Angle -- ten days before the midterms -- Laura Ingraham put the hypothetical to Mike Davis: founder and president of the Article III Project, former chief counsel for nominations to the Senate Judiciary Committee's Republicans, a clerk for Neil Gorsuch. What happens to the Second Amendment if Democrats pack the Supreme Court? Davis needed three words: "It would be gone." Then he said the rest: they would take away our God-given right to keep and bear arms, and they would claim the Second Amendment covers only the National Guard. Hyperbole? Only if you don't know the math or the history. Both cut his way. The math behind "gone." District of Columbia v. Heller (2008) recognized an individual right to keep a handgun at home, 5-4\. The Court described the right as pre-existing -- the amendment protects a right it did not create, the same Creator-endowed logic as the Declaration -- which is why Davis says God-given. But it was close. Four dissents argued the right belongs to the militias -- the "organized militia" the federal government reorganized as the National Guard by the Militia Act of 1903 and the National Defense Act of 1916. Justice John Paul Stevens wrote that dissent, and in March 2018 he published a New York Times op-ed titled, without euphemism, "Repeal the Second Amendment." McDonald (2010) applied the right to the states, 5-4\. Bruen (2022) extended it outside the home, 6-3. The anti-Heller bloc currently numbers three -- the Court's three Democratic appointees. Add four seats and it is seven to six. Heller, McDonald, and Bruen flip in a single term; D.C.-style handgun bans are constitutional again; the militia reading becomes the law of the land. Hillary Clinton herself once called D.C.'s ban "reasonable" -- a polite way of dissenting from Heller. That is what "gone" means: not a repeal passed by Congress and ratified by thirty-eight states, but seven justices declaring that the words mean what the dissidents always said they meant -- Guard service and a permission slip. Repealing the text is impossible. Repainting its meaning takes a majority of both chambers and a willing president. The thirteen-circuits excuse. Days before the segment, on a podcast, Clinton supplied the justification the packing push had been missing: "You know, it used to be that you'd have one justice for each circuit. We now have 13 circuits, we should have 13 justices." Add her headline caveat -- "we should seriously look at expanding the court while the Democrats are in power" -- and note that Elizabeth Warren backs the idea, while Jim Clyburn said on Meet the Press that "we ought to expand." Davis destroyed this in about thirty seconds, and the historical record supports every syllable. There have been nine justices since 1869. Yes, for most of the Court's first century the justices rode circuit -- and while they did, Congress did grow the bench alongside the circuits: six justices and three circuits in 1789; a seventh of each in 1807; the eighth and ninth in 1837; a tenth circuit in 1863. But in 1891 Congress created the Courts of Appeals so the justices would not have to ride, and by 1911 circuit-riding was formally abolished. The workload rationale died with it. Then comes the proof. Congress kept adding circuits and never added a justice. The Tenth Circuit was created in 1929 -- the bench stayed at nine. The Federal Circuit in 1982 -- nine. Of today's thirteen circuits, two (the D.C. Circuit and the Federal Circuit) aren't geographic circuits at all. One justice per circuit was never a constitutional rule or a statute; it was a workload arrangement from the horseback era that ended 135 years ago. Clinton was quoting an administrative convenience of 1837 as if it were a principle of 2026. The circuits are geography. The bench is not. The question that ends the debate. If the court truly needs thirteen -- if it's arithmetic about circuits -- why is no Democrat demanding thirteen right now, with a Republican president and a Republican Senate? Because the demand follows power, not principle. The last time Democrats held the House, the Senate, and the White House with a 6-3 court, Senator Ed Markey and Representative Hank Johnson introduced the Judiciary Act of 2021: exactly four seats, a thirteen-justice court. It went nowhere -- the filibuster stood, Manchin and Sinema stood with it -- and the number quietly disappeared until this month's election-eve revival. To be fair to Clinton, "look at" and "see if we could make it work" is softer than enactment. But that is the tell. A principle doesn't wait to see if it can work; a device does. The device resurfaces only when the court's composition is the prize. Four votes. Franklin Roosevelt wanted six extra seats in 1937 -- a court of fifteen -- and the Senate Judiciary Committee killed the plan in July, 10-8\. The modern ask is smaller and surgical: four seats turn every contested line -- Heller, Bruen, the rest of the 5-4s and 6-3s -- into seven-vote majorities overnight. Not reform. The minimum winning number. That is Davis's real answer, and Ingraham's monologue -- which RealClearPolitics clipped under the title "The Democrats Stampede To Pack the Supreme Court" -- framed it: a court you can pack is a court you can own. Nine justices have held the text above simple majorities since 1869. The circuits figure is the fig leaf; four is the operative number; and "It would be gone" is the price of admission. ? | [](https://substack.com/redirect/56ce6012-f6d0-4c48-b2e6-0db3b4e9cf64?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|

Of course, no one cares about my vote, because I live in New York where most contests are pre-decided by the time the general election arrives. All eyes will be on Congressional races and Senate contests in Texas, Michigan, Maine, Ohio, and even unlikely places like Kansas, Alaska, Montana, South Dakota and Idaho. I'm also intrigued by gubernatorial races in Ohio, Florida and Iowa. The question on everyone's mind is on who wins the House and the Senate and whether Democrats will be in position to stifle Trump and the Republicans before the clock turns to '28.
I got asked on TV the other day whether Democrats win both the House and the Senate. I think they do. Trump and J.D. Vance have Kansas and Montana on their travel schedules. That's a schedule of trying to stop the bleeding. Trump's approval rating is a historically low 32% and even the South Dakota Senator Mike Rounds scrubbed the Trump language from his materials. You know you're doing badly when Republicans in South Dakota are running away from you.
In my mind, the major question is whether Republicans accept the results. They've been trying to muddy the water in various ways, and AI bots hacking results is a genuine possibility. The Trump crew isn't prone to accepting defeat. Will they accept the one that is coming their way tomorrow?
You have an unhappy populace, an unpopular war, stubborn inflation, anxiety about AI, and an administration that seems almost intentionally petty and tone-deaf. So I expect a blowout night for Democrats tomorrow night, including victories in places that have been pipe dreams for decades. Americans are as ornery as I've ever seen, and it's an anti-incumbent wave.
If the results are what I expect, the Democrats will soon begin crowing about how everyone likes and believes in them again, which unfortunately for them couldn't be further from the truth. A majority of Americans - 55% - disapprove of the Democratic Party while only 40% approve. It's kind of tough to make a case for being the governing majority when most Americans don't like or trust you before you say a word. Indeed, some of the most successful candidates of this cycle, like James Talarico and Rob Sand, go out of their way to separate themselves from the two-party system.
It's also why we've seen Independent Senate candidates running competitively in Idaho, South Dakota, Montana, and Nebraska, with all of those states requiring investment on the part of the Republicans to play defense in states that most would consider deep red and non-battlegrounds. This was the case I made back in 2021: that you need a third force in American politics that energizes the growing plurality - 45% or so - that consider ourselves Independents. I've campaigned with each of these Senate candidates and dearly hope that one or more of them breaks through. What a story and victory that would be! If you feel like giving some last minute money or energy, [Brian Bengs](https://substack.com/redirect/2d76c235-082c-4232-9739-daa1e33b863f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), [Todd Achilles](https://substack.com/redirect/2b0bb478-55b8-45ce-a3fe-df45e63b4947?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), and/or [Seth Bodnar](https://substack.com/redirect/17955d93-c4c0-4e36-834f-53074bedda85?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), or [Forward](https://substack.com/redirect/dc34c43a-9f1e-4c29-ba58-4d5f81898fcc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) could definitely use them, and the math says that your dollar will go a much longer way with these scrappy upstarts in remote locations.
My trip to South Dakota last week was a reminder of how big and diverse the country is. Normal people don't get caught up in the news cycle social media firestorm of the day. They just want a sense that their lives and their kids' lives might get a little better. I think their vote tomorrow is going to send a clear message.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/a8a5b408-46a2-457c-a7ea-b878c9d303c2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
I'm doing media interviews on various channels on Election Day and then heading to a Forward Party Election Night event in Baltimore. Get your vote in and pull up a chair, because the next 48 hours are going to be history in the making.
[Offline](https://substack.com/redirect/cebb1fde-b548-44c8-af05-35936d0d28b8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) returns to New York City on Thursday - you can turn your phone off for a few hours and unwind from the week that was. clean_body: Election Day is finally here tomorrow. | | ---|---|--- | | | Forwarded this email? ? for more | | ---|---|--- * | | | Nov 2 | | | | | | | | | | | | Election Day is finally here tomorrow. Did you get your vote in? I voted last week early. | | ---|---|--- Of course, no one cares about my vote, because I live in New York where most contests are pre-decided by the time the general election arrives. All eyes will be on Congressional races and Senate contests in Texas, Michigan, Maine, Ohio, and even unlikely places like Kansas, Alaska, Montana, South Dakota and Idaho. I'm also intrigued by gubernatorial races in Ohio, Florida and Iowa. The question on everyone's mind is on who wins the House and the Senate and whether Democrats will be in position to stifle Trump and the Republicans before the clock turns to '28. I got asked on TV the other day whether Democrats win both the House and the Senate. I think they do. Trump and J.D. Vance have Kansas and Montana on their travel schedules. That's a schedule of trying to stop the bleeding. Trump's approval rating is a historically low 32% and even the South Dakota Senator Mike Rounds scrubbed the Trump language from his materials. You know you're doing badly when Republicans in South Dakota are running away from you. In my mind, the major question is whether Republicans accept the results. They've been trying to muddy the water in various ways, and AI bots hacking results is a genuine possibility. The Trump crew isn't prone to accepting defeat. Will they accept the one that is coming their way tomorrow? You have an unhappy populace, an unpopular war, stubborn inflation, anxiety about AI, and an administration that seems almost intentionally petty and tone-deaf. So I expect a blowout night for Democrats tomorrow night, including victories in places that have been pipe dreams for decades. Americans are as ornery as I've ever seen, and it's an anti-incumbent wave. If the results are what I expect, the Democrats will soon begin crowing about how everyone likes and believes in them again, which unfortunately for them couldn't be further from the truth. A majority of Americans - 55% - disapprove of the Democratic Party while only 40% approve. It's kind of tough to make a case for being the governing majority when most Americans don't like or trust you before you say a word. Indeed, some of the most successful candidates of this cycle, like James Talarico and Rob Sand, go out of their way to separate themselves from the two-party system. It's also why we've seen Independent Senate candidates running competitively in Idaho, South Dakota, Montana, and Nebraska, with all of those states requiring investment on the part of the Republicans to play defense in states that most would consider deep red and non-battlegrounds. This was the case I made back in 2021: that you need a third force in American politics that energizes the growing plurality - 45% or so - that consider ourselves Independents. I've campaigned with each of these Senate candidates and dearly hope that one or more of them breaks through. What a story and victory that would be! If you feel like giving some last minute money or energy, , , and/or , or could definitely use them, and the math says that your dollar will go a much longer way with these scrappy upstarts in remote locations. My trip to South Dakota last week was a reminder of how big and diverse the country is. Normal people don't get caught up in the news cycle social media firestorm of the day. They just want a sense that their lives and their kids' lives might get a little better. I think their vote tomorrow is going to send a clear message. | | ---|---|--- I'm doing media interviews on various channels on Election Day and then heading to a Forward Party Election Night event in Baltimore. [ stdin# ]Jocelyn Benson for Governor
