clean_body: Don’t get pulled into the noise. Lock in. Focus on one thing: getting every Democrat in Michigan to the polls on Tuesday. | | | | | Peter, there's a lot of noise out there right now. We can’t be distracted. Some people would love for the last days of this race to be about politicians. Who said what. Who's mad at whom. Screenshots and hot takes. I will not be distracted. Every minute spent talking about politicians is a minute taken from the people this election is really about: working Michiganders. — This election is about the dad I met who told me his kid is really good at baseball but can't play next year because he just can't afford it. — This election is about everyone who's been told to wait for relief to “trickle down” while groceries, rent, and healthcare slip further out of reach. — And it's about people far beyond our state. Because Michigan will decide control of the United States Senate. A Democratic Senate is how we put a check on Donald Trump's power. Mike Rogers, Trump's handpicked candidate, wants to be one more vote for the same billionaire agenda that's been fleecing Michigan for decades. Please don’t get distracted by the political drama. I promise you I won’t. Election Day is Tuesday. Several polls show us statistically tied with Mike Rogers. In 2024, the Senate race here came down to 20,217 votes. I’m told there's still time to put our final get-out-the-vote ads in front of Michigan voters, but only if we have the cash to run them right now. | If you've stored your payment information with ActBlue Express, your donation will process immediately and be split between Abdul El-Sayed and DLCC PAC. | | | | | | Let them have the drama. If we turn out every Democratic voter in Wisconsin, we’re going to win in a landslide. | | | | [](https://click.actionnetwork.org/ss/c/u001.iIBo0N5fSFzEFL40Tn-vtbMETCUYClkOrOh9-SNJfquchf2e3e-bIm5hAkq2zKIje5ZlElB9ot5ZI8yW4fgOALJQAT7uIIIYwY2Mj6-d9DJq3ZgAnWd4qCwlf-wDGwFGIlal8xGmnJViUlm1LKIx844rzKJbu-FmA83kA66wvTQuM2H3qieTogVkcXU6AAkKKKF1UcyxC8Kek3h0HEK5IIfli_rGxPDJrcVcaXkyXlyK9WR42KO51WlSNSfwDb7JMwS7hOSKgYISVLWMqhQtiO_2Gf6rFlLDgXcLAb7iiAKyzUJLZEJhuq4t35aiOzn48gOKBf1G2NnXcGBtZZvbKTA__tVe9xSfiKrSwbT-H-UdgwisTPCKNE8qas-cS776RI4wNENYYSbxElolqr2Tps7kvwhDB5p0TSiR2IIe_rvruNn3LTd6HANHbIWljqe6DZPvNvgucGkFss6DOP1zjPup-vnyzyE17x4IvyW0gBc/4ve/8vG-OqaMRxOXwbt6HoolvA/h0/h001.Frtpn8ETsECAeGDXk8uvOSffq0bBxss7ml_WX1aTVMU) Hey, Derek, it’s Ben Wikler, former WisDems chair. We have ONE DAY left. And the fight we’ve all been fighting—sixteen years of organizing to win a Democratic governorship and state legislature in Wisconsin—is on a knife’s edge. The election-denying billionaires on the right know the stakes in this election. That’s why they’ve poured over $34 million into helping Tom Tiffany. But there’s one thing they didn’t count on. You. You’ve powered Democratic victories year over year in the hardest-fought state in the country. You beat Scott Walker, you flipped the state Supreme Court majority, you ended gerrymandered maps. And in these final days, the power is in your hands to ensure that David Crowley and the Dems win it all. If we turn out every Democratic voter in Wisconsin, we’re going to win in a landslide. **[Can you split $10 right now between WisDems and Battleground Wisconsin to help turn out every last Democrat in the state?](https://click.actionnetwork.org/ss/c/u001.iIBo0N5fSFzEFL40Tn-vtbMETCUYClkOrOh9-SNJfquchf2e3e-bIm5hAkq2zKIje5ZlElB9ot5ZI8yW4fgOALJQAT7uIIIYwY2Mj6-d9DJq3ZgAnWd4qCwlf-wDGwFGIlal8xGmnJViUlm1LKIx844rzKJbu-FmA83kA66wvTQuM2H3qieTogVkcXU6AAkKKKF1UcyxC8Kek3h0HEK5ICYagiLOLCVE_7MoMFzDAUNCsty7JCboR-2jSZBO1FIPSLh-fKviXcU0uwRybcPenXKOMNwM-ek5j-vfLui7j9hPGiqTXyzkg9ZTFprCceBh0-8uFUyGY6JrTHK4vRZAMFGC_ywjgulWVPjC8g3b9dCbX70ioATG7qLbipyFVctdysqPWhzeuSGsj_eQUdO6vqFcGogguVQUAsZhUkaNlG_ZgQX40EtXw6azPnZLgDSj4hHenLl4neKdlqf2zdpCuB72rpky5zXlbkJ9vZGrFSo/4ve/8vG-OqaMRxOXwbt6HoolvA/h1/h001.FM31haHMKmqNxEMscsmJlKUky9ovyGp-esip1hVMLnc)** We’ve seen this movie before: Elon Musk tried to buy the state Supreme Court race in 2025. We threw him out of the state and elected Susan Crawford by ten percentage points. Now, Elon Musk is back—and along with him, three more MAGA mega-billionaires who are flooding the airwaves with ads and flying canvassers in from Texas to knock on Wisconsinites’ doors. But you know our secret weapon: people power. Our organizers are working with teams of volunteers in every corner of the state, right now, to talk to their neighbors, make phone calls, and build a blue wave from the bottom up. I was proud to support that grassroots operation when I was chair. Devin Remiker and the whole WisDems team are doing an amazing job now to organize their way to even higher heights. The GOP has more money, but at the grassroots level, they’re not even close to what you’ve helped build. Now we have to run through the tape. Your money pays for (expensive!) gas mileage as organizers drive from canvass launch to canvass launch, for clipboards for volunteers, and for printing costs for door hangers. clean_body: If we turn out every Democratic voter in Wisconsin, we’re going to win in a landslide. | | | | Hey, Derek, it’s Ben Wikler, former WisDems chair. We have ONE DAY left. And the fight we’ve all been fighting—sixteen years of organizing to win a Democratic governorship and state legislature in Wisconsin—is on a knife’s edge. The election-denying billionaires on the right know the stakes in this election. That’s why they’ve poured over $34 million into helping Tom Tiffany. But there’s one thing they didn’t count on. You. You’ve powered Democratic victories year over year in the hardest-fought state in the country. You beat Scott Walker, you flipped the state Supreme Court majority, you ended gerrymandered maps. And in these final days, the power is in your hands to ensure that David Crowley and the Dems win it all. If we turn out every Democratic voter in Wisconsin, we’re going to win in a landslide. We’ve seen this movie before: Elon Musk tried to buy the state Supreme Court race in 2025. We threw him out of the state and elected Susan Crawford by ten percentage points. Now, Elon Musk is back—and along with him, three more MAGA mega-billionaires who are flooding the airwaves with ads and flying canvassers in from Texas to knock on Wisconsinites’ doors. But you know our secret weapon: people power. Our organizers are working with teams of volunteers in every corner of the state, right now, to talk to their neighbors, make phone calls, and build a blue wave from the bottom up. I was proud to support that grassroots operation when I was chair. Devin Remiker and the whole WisDems team are doing an amazing job now to organize their way to even higher heights. The GOP has more money, but at the grassroots level, they’re not even close to what you’ve helped build. Now we have to run through the tape. Your money pays for (expensive!) gas mileage as organizers drive from canvass launch to canvass launch, for clipboards for volunteers, and for printing costs for door hangers. body:
[1]Talarico for Texas

We wanted to make sure you saw this note below from James. A donation
today is still important because we spent into the red, and our
fundraising is pacing behind.

We’re talking about scaling back when we really need to focus on turning
out Texans. [ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261102-1-ak&t=1001&akid=1188%2E1347274%2EKEI_fs ]Please donate $5 or any amount you can
afford.

[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261102-1-ak&t=1002&akid=1188%2E1347274%2EKEI_fs ]CONTRIBUTE

We’re getting a lot of questions about whether or not a donation today can
really make any difference.

And the answer is, in no uncertain terms, absolutely. Here’s why:

When we made our budget, we had to look at historical data and fundraising
trends. It gave us an idea of what we could raise and how we needed to
manage our cash flow.

And what you see in every election cycle is that there is a significant
amount of money raised in the final few days before Election Day. So you
need to take that into account as you make spending decisions.

Smart campaigns will spend a bit into the red — knowing that money will
come through. That’s what we did. Not egregiously — a responsible amount
based on what our data suggests we’re likely to raise.

But it’s not an insignificant amount either. It makes me a bit
uncomfortable how much, but to be as transparent with you as I can —
historical data and our own metrics showed we should raise more in the
final three days of this campaign than we raised in the entire month of
October 2025. Wild, right?

So right now, we’re in the red. There are bills due tomorrow and Tuesday
that we have to pay, and if we don’t see the money that we projected
rolling in, then we’ll have to quickly cancel a bunch of ads and
organizing work to get refunds. It could mean our campaign goes dark in
the final hours of the race — when the undecided voters who plan to vote
on Election Day will make up their minds.

[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261102-1-ak&t=1003&akid=1188%2E1347274%2EKEI_fs ]So yes, your donation today can make a difference, so I am personally
asking you to consider making a contribution if you can.

[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261102-1-ak&t=1004&akid=1188%2E1347274%2EKEI_fs ]CONTRIBUTE

I know there are still some folks who will have questions. I hear it every
day: “But James, haven’t you raised a record-breaking amount of money?
Isn’t that already enough?”

And I hear you. I too wish that elections did not cost this much. It’s
gross, and I would love to watch the Longhorns play without being
inundated with political attack ads.

But history says this kind of spending is what it takes for Democrats to
flip a Senate seat like this. In 2020, Jon Ossoff needed more than $150
million to flip Georgia — which has a population a third of the size of
Texas.

On top of that, Elon Musk swooped in and almost single-handedly made this
the most expensive non-presidential race in American history. He
personally bankrolled the operation to rescue Ken Paxton.

And the spending is entirely lopsided. The next most expensive races have
had far more parity between Democrats and Republicans — while we’re being
basically obliterated. Ken Paxton has a massive spending advantage behind
him. His allies are spending $200 million more than ours.

It is likely once all of the data shakes out that I will have more money
spent against me than any non-presidential candidate in American history.

Sorry to inundate you with data and explanations, but I thought you
deserved candor.

The truth is every dollar we have raised has been spent already. It was
the only way to avoid an unspent surplus. That would be a disservice to
everyone who invested their hopes and resources in this movement.

There’s nothing that would make me feel worse than someone giving their
hard-earned money to our cause just to have it go unspent because we
weren’t smart enough to plan ahead.

But it does mean that every dollar we raise right now is making an impact.
It’s winning votes and turning out Democrats.

[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261102-1-ak&t=1005&akid=1188%2E1347274%2EKEI_fs ]So if you care about taking back Texas, I hope you will consider making
a contribution today to help us win. It’d mean a lot to me.

[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261102-1-ak&t=1006&akid=1188%2E1347274%2EKEI_fs ]CONTRIBUTE

James

[ https://act.jamestalarico.com/go/512?c0=jt-em-2026q4.erR9_P&refcode=em261102-1-ak&t=1007&akid=1188%2E1347274%2EKEI_fs ]'New York Times: In Texas, Talarico Inspires a Recurring Blue-Tinted
Dream In the go-big-or-go-home collective consciousness of Texas, no
ambition is deemed too reckless, no daydream too wild. Save perhaps one.
It is the idea, fantastical to many as it is irresistible to others, that
the Democrats will win a statewide race in Texas for the first time in 32
years. According to the latest New York Times/Siena University poll of the
race for U.S. Senate, James Talarico, a 37-year-old state legislator seen
by national Democrats as one of the breakout stars of this cycle, is ahead
of his Republican rival, Ken Paxton, the state’s scandal-plagued attorney
general, by six points. The poll was conducted from Sept. 21 to Sept. 30.
A survey from mid-September, the ReconMR/Siena Research Institute poll,
also showed the Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Gina Hinojosa, four
points ahead of the three-term G.O.P. incumbent, Greg Abbott, the most
dominant political figure in Texas. Cue the fluttering heartbeats. Cue, as
well, the eye-rolls. Given how thoroughly Republicans have dominated the
state, and how the hopes of Democrats have repeatedly crashed, some Texas
pollsters remain skeptical. “At some point, you do get conditioned by all
that’s happened in the past,” said James Henson, the director of the
University of Texas at Austin’s Texas Politics Project. “I mean, you look
at the trends and you have to admit that something’s going on. But you
still don’t want to believe your lying eyes, because you’ve been burned
for so long.” Mr. Henson was referring to the perennial spectacle of
much-ballyhooed Texas Democratic aspirants face-planting against the Lone
Star State’s red wall. First came Tony Sanchez Jr., the swaggering and
self-funding Laredo oilman whom Gov. Rick Perry dispatched in 2002 by an
18-point margin. Next was the state senator Wendy Davis, who attracted
worldwide attention for her filibuster in the Texas Legislature against an
anti-abortion measure but whom Mr. Abbott demolished by 20 points in 2014.
Finally, the El Paso congressman Beto O’Rourke came up 2.6 points short of
defeating Senator Ted Cruz in 2018 but then suffered a 10-point loss to
Mr. Abbott four years later. Even with the awareness of such humiliations,
Democrats find themselves maintaining that 2026 could, at long last, be
the year. President Trump’s deep unpopularity and the prospect of a blue
wave could, they insist, extend into the state he won by nearly 14 points
in 2024. According to a September survey conducted by Texas Southern
University, Mr. Trump is seven points underwater in Texas. Mr. Talarico
has run an energetic and well-financed campaign, while Mr. Paxton has
staged far fewer public events and has had to rely on outside groups to
fund an attack-ad blitzkrieg against his Democratic opponent. Mr. Abbott,
meanwhile, has outspent Ms. Hinojosa by a 10-to-one ratio, yet has been
unable to build an insurmountable lead. “People have vastly underestimated
Gina,” said Ms. Davis, now a political consultant and a senior adviser to
Planned Parenthood Texas Votes, an advocacy organization. “Dollar for
dollar, she’s running the best statewide campaign we’ve ever seen.” Such
optimism stands in defiance of the political axiom that Texas is where
idealistic Democrats go to be mugged by reality. The party’s demise there
is not a product of ill fortune, Mr. Henson said. “Governor Abbott has
built an impressive election machine that has benefited state-level
Republicans again and again for a decade and a half,” he said. “And the
Democratic machinery here is almost nonexistent.” A ‘Hollowing-Out’ I have
written about the politics of my native state at regular intervals for
more than three decades. After watching the Democrats’ century-long rule
in Texas come to a decisive end with Gov. Ann Richards’s loss to George W.
Bush in 1994, I saw the party descend into atrophy in which failure begot
more failure. “The 30-year drought has done a lot of things,” said Luke
Warford, the chairman of the Travis County Democratic Party and the
founder of the Agave Democratic Infrastructure Fund. “It’s kept donors on
the sidelines, which makes a lot of potentially good candidates not run
because there’s no belief they can win. And it also makes a lot of really
talented staff leave to find better-paying work in true battleground
states.” The Democratic Party has no counterpart to Mr. Abbott, and hasn’t
since 1993, when Senator Lloyd Bentsen moved to Washington to join
President Bill Clinton’s cabinet. Its weaknesses are even more glaring
farther down the hierarchy. In recent elections, as many as one-third of
state races have gone uncontested by Democrats. One-fifth of the party’s
county chairs and two-thirds of its precinct chairs have been left
unfilled. Until last year, the state party had a negative operating
budget. As the veteran Democratic consultant Matt Angle observed, “There’s
been a hollowing-out of the party.” Still, those of us who recall the
satisfied sense of invincibility among Texas Democrats after roughly a
century of one-party rule have detected similar signs of overconfidence
among the state’s ruling party. The party’s rightward tilt, increasingly
forceful with each legislative session, reached its apotheosis in March,
with Mr. Paxton’s primary victory over the more moderate Republican
four-term incumbent, Senator John Cornyn. Mr. Paxton, a close ally of Mr.
Trump’s, was impeached by the Republican-controlled State House (and later
acquitted by the State Senate) in 2023 over allegations that included
bribery. He was also accused by his wife of adultery. Mr. Trump endorsed
him anyway, all but guaranteeing his landslide primary triumph over Mr.
Cornyn but in the process testing the allegiance of center-right Texans.
In similar fashion, the Texas G.O.P. is in danger of losing many Latino
voters who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 after years of siding with
Democrats. “We adopted a lazy way of campaigning that bit us on the ass,
and we’ve learned from that,” Mr. O’Rourke said. “Now it’s the Republicans
who’ve gotten really lazy and complacent and comfortable.” Signs of
Republican Overreach Simply spending one week driving through the vastness
of Texas, as I did in September, is all it takes to appreciate an underdog
party’s uphill battle. The state’s 32 million residents are spread across
20 media markets, many of them distinct ecosystems, from the urban colossi
of Houston and the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex to the oil patch of the
Texas Panhandle to the Latino-dominated borderlands of the Rio Grande
Valley. “When national donors are deciding where to invest, they look at a
place like Iowa, where $5 million can fully fund a race,” said Katherine
Fischer, the director of the Texas Majority PAC, which was established by
the liberal philanthropist Soros family. “That’s why Texas is always at
the bottom of their list. It’s just so damned big.” Reaching so many
markets presents a daunting challenge for an upstart candidate like Ms.
Hinojosa, a state representative from the border city of Brownsville.
“There’s still 20 percent of the electorate that doesn’t know who I am,”
she said in an interview in mid-September. To date, Ms. Hinojosa’s
campaign has said that it has raised about $20 million. For his part, Mr.
Talarico spent about $30 million earlier this year to introduce himself
statewide as a man of Christian faith and a member of the Texas House with
a record of supporting bipartisan legislation. Since that time, however,
Mr. Paxton and his associates have invested more than $100 million in an
effort to redefine his opponent as “radical” and “weird,” with ads that
quote from remarks Mr. Talarico made several years ago (and later
renounced) suggesting that “God is nonbinary” and that there are six
biological sexes. Mr. Paxton and his allies have at times questioned Mr.
Talarico’s manhood and even his Christianity, an effort to jolt the
sensibilities of a state prone to mythologizing godly and masculine
archetypes. “How they’re negatively defining Talarico is kind of a
bank-shot way of saying that he’s not a true Texas conservative,” Mr.
Henson said. Whether money can overwhelm conditions on the ground is the
riddle looming over the Texas races. In the border city of Laredo, which
Mr. Trump won in 2024 — the first time a Republican had done so in over a
century — signs of buyer’s remorse are evident. Arrests by Immigration and
Customs Enforcement agents in Laredo were higher in July than in any other
American city. Mr. Trump’s erratic trade policies have further created
instability at the city’s port of entry. While acknowledging the economic
concerns that many border residents share, Adrian Zapata, a business
executive in the health industry who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, said in
an interview that the negative ads against Mr. Talarico were resonating
with some of his family members. “They see Talarico as an ultraliberal,”
he said. “They’re done with the ‘they/them.’ They’re going to vote for
Paxton just because of that.” As for Mr. Zapata, “I’m not ready to vote
for Talarico,” he said. “But I don’t like Paxton. He’s never done anything
for South Texas, and his personal and business dealings have hurt him a
lot with folks down here.” There is a similarly muddled electoral picture
in the cattle country of deep West Texas adjacent to Big Bend National
Park. Mr. Trump and Mr. Abbott have aggressively championed a border wall
and artificial intelligence data centers, both of which threaten to
disrupt the region’s pastoral ethos. A coalition of more than 200
landowners has sued the federal government over the border wall, while
other residents have circulated a petition to protest the construction of
a new data center near Fort Stockton. George Johnson, a cattle feed
operator in Alpine, waved off such concerns, saying: “Folks worrying about
data centers were also worried when the internet got started. It’s
Talarico who scares me to death, him and all that socialist talk.” Others
in this largely conservative region harbor the view that Republicans have
failed to make good on their promises. Thaddeus Cleveland, the Republican
sheriff of Terrell County, said that both he and his county had voted for
Mr. Trump in 2024, but added, “Everything he campaigned on, we’re seeing
the opposite of, like going to war.” Sheriff Cleveland predicted that the
negative campaign ads by the Republicans would not factor as significantly
into the votes of his neighbors as “the price of groceries and gas, which
are compounded here because we’re so far from everywhere else.” But it is
in purple Tarrant County, dominated by Fort Worth, where the party could
pay the price for having potentially overestimated its mandate from the
voters. Conservative leaders have cut funds for nonprofits that aid
at-risk children, subjected school library books to right-wing litmus
tests and eliminated free bus rides to polling stations in poor
neighborhoods. “The far-right leaders here have implemented Project 2025
on a county level,” said Alisa Simmons, a Democrat and county commissioner
who is running to unseat the conservative county judge, Tim O’Hare. In an
early sign this year that area Republicans may be out of step with Tarrant
County’s constituents, a Democratic aviation machinist and union leader,
Taylor Rehmet, defeated Leigh Wambsganss, a well-funded Republican
Christian activist who led the conservative takeover of several metroplex
school boards. He won by 14 points in a January special election for a
State Senate seat covering a region that Mr. Trump won by 17 points in
2024. A ‘Gradualist’ Theory Which party prevails in Texas is a complicated
riddle. Historically a low-turnout state — it ranked second to last in the
2024 election, ahead of only Arkansas — Texas held a primary in March that
saw nearly one in four voters showing up to the polls, a modern record for
midterm participation, with Democrats slightly outpacing Republicans. A
few factors could conspire to thwart a blue wave in Texas. As of 2020,
straight-ticket voting is no longer possible in the state, which could
impact the mostly Democratic urban counties where that practice has
frequently been used by voters in past elections. Texas is one of only
eight states that lack universal online registration, while voting by mail
is also highly restricted. In January, Mr. Abbott turned over the state’s
list of approximately 18.7 million registered voters to the Trump
administration, and 1.2 million of them have subsequently been put on the
“suspense list” because their addresses have not been verified. The recent
shuttering of nearly one-third of Tarrant County’s polling sites by its
Republican-controlled county commission is particularly worrisome for
Democrats. “The reason we’ve lost these statewide races in the past is
because we’ve never gotten enough out of Tarrant County to overcome the
margins in rural Texas,” Ms. Davis said of the turnout. “If we don’t get
it to 53 or 54 percent this November, it’s game over. James and Gina can’t
win.” But the state’s Republicans have reasons of their own to be fretful.
Partly because of the recruitment efforts of the Texas Majority PAC and
Blueprint Texas, a down-ballot candidate support organization co-founded
by Ms. Davis earlier this year, the Democrats are fielding a full slate in
all 150 state races for the first time in a half-century. Though many of
these aspirants face long odds, their presence on the ballot could
energize the Democrats in predominantly conservative regions who have not
bothered to turn out in the past. “If we win on Nov. 3, most of those
names running down-ballot in really tough areas like East Texas and the
Hill Country and the Panhandle will be responsible,” Mr. O’Rourke said.
Mr. Henson added that while he remained skeptical about Democratic
enthusiasm being sufficient to carry the day for Mr. Talarico, he also
doubted that a last-minute avalanche of negative ads would prove decisive
for Mr. Paxton. “At a certain point, there’s diminishing impact once you
get past an absurd level of spending,” he said. Rather than project a
winner in November, Mr. Henson said he felt more comfortable embracing a
“gradualist” theory, one in which Texas does not become blue overnight,
but instead competitive. “Even if Talarico loses by a Beto-like margin,”
he said, “the next cycle is a presidential election, where Trump likely
won’t be popular and Democratic turnout will be higher. So there are
reasons for Texas Democrats to be optimistic.”'

One-fifth of the party’s county chairs and two-thirds of its precinct chairs have been left unfilled. Until last year, the state party had a negative operating budget. As the veteran Democratic consultant Matt Angle observed, “There’s been a hollowing-out of the party.” Still, those of us who recall the satisfied sense of invincibility among Texas Democrats after roughly a century of one-party rule have detected similar signs of overconfidence among the state’s ruling party. The party’s rightward tilt, increasingly forceful with each legislative session, reached its apotheosis in March, with Mr. Paxton’s primary victory over the more moderate Republican four-term incumbent, Senator John Cornyn. Mr. Paxton, a close ally of Mr. Trump’s, was impeached by the Republican-controlled State House (and later acquitted by the State Senate) in 2023 over allegations that included bribery. He was also accused by his wife of adultery. Mr. Trump endorsed him anyway, all but guaranteeing his landslide primary triumph over Mr. Cornyn but in the process testing the allegiance of center-right Texans. In similar fashion, the Texas G.O.P. is in danger of losing many Latino voters who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 after years of siding with Democrats. “We adopted a lazy way of campaigning that bit us on the ass, and we’ve learned from that,” Mr. O’Rourke said. “Now it’s the Republicans who’ve gotten really lazy and complacent and comfortable.” Signs of Republican Overreach Simply spending one week driving through the vastness of Texas, as I did in September, is all it takes to appreciate an underdog party’s uphill battle. The state’s 32 million residents are spread across 20 media markets, many of them distinct ecosystems, from the urban colossi of Houston and the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex to the oil patch of the Texas Panhandle to the Latino-dominated borderlands of the Rio Grande Valley. “When national donors are deciding where to invest, they look at a place like Iowa, where $5 million can fully fund a race,” said Katherine Fischer, the director of the Texas Majority PAC, which was established by the liberal philanthropist Soros family. “That’s why Texas is always at the bottom of their list. It’s just so damned big.” Reaching so many markets presents a daunting challenge for an upstart candidate like Ms. Hinojosa, a state representative from the border city of Brownsville. “There’s still 20 percent of the electorate that doesn’t know who I am,” she said in an interview in mid-September. To date, Ms. Hinojosa’s campaign has said that it has raised about $20 million. For his part, Mr. Talarico spent about $30 million earlier this year to introduce himself statewide as a man of Christian faith and a member of the Texas House with a record of supporting bipartisan legislation. Since that time, however, Mr. Paxton and his associates have invested more than $100 million in an effort to redefine his opponent as “radical” and “weird,” with ads that quote from remarks Mr. Talarico made several years ago (and later renounced) suggesting that “God is nonbinary” and that there are six biological sexes. Mr. Paxton and his allies have at times questioned Mr. Talarico’s manhood and even his Christianity, an effort to jolt the sensibilities of a state prone to mythologizing godly and masculine archetypes. “How they’re negatively defining Talarico is kind of a bank-shot way of saying that he’s not a true Texas conservative,” Mr. Henson said. Whether money can overwhelm conditions on the ground is the riddle looming over the Texas races. In the border city of Laredo, which Mr. Trump won in 2024 — the first time a Republican had done so in over a century — signs of buyer’s remorse are evident. Arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Laredo were higher in July than in any other American city. Mr. Trump’s erratic trade policies have further created instability at the city’s port of entry. While acknowledging the economic concerns that many border residents share, Adrian Zapata, a business executive in the health industry who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, said in an interview that the negative ads against Mr. Talarico were resonating with some of his family members. “They see Talarico as an ultraliberal,” he said. “They’re done with the ‘they/them.’ They’re going to vote for Paxton just because of that.” As for Mr. Zapata, “I’m not ready to vote for Talarico,” he said. “But I don’t like Paxton. He’s never done anything for South Texas, and his personal and business dealings have hurt him a lot with folks down here.” There is a similarly muddled electoral picture in the cattle country of deep West Texas adjacent to Big Bend National Park. Mr. Trump and Mr. Abbott have aggressively championed a border wall and artificial intelligence data centers, both of which threaten to disrupt the region’s pastoral ethos. A coalition of more than 200 landowners has sued the federal government over the border wall, while other residents have circulated a petition to protest the construction of a new data center near Fort Stockton. George Johnson, a cattle feed operator in Alpine, waved off such concerns, saying: “Folks worrying about data centers were also worried when the internet got started. It’s Talarico who scares me to death, him and all that socialist talk.” Others in this largely conservative region harbor the view that Republicans have failed to make good on their promises. Thaddeus Cleveland, the Republican sheriff of Terrell County, said that both he and his county had voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, but added, “Everything he campaigned on, we’re seeing the opposite of, like going to war.” Sheriff Cleveland predicted that the negative campaign ads by the Republicans would not factor as significantly into the votes of his neighbors as “the price of groceries and gas, which are compounded here because we’re so far from everywhere else.” But it is in purple Tarrant County, dominated by Fort Worth, where the party could pay the price for having potentially overestimated its mandate from the voters. Conservative leaders have cut funds for nonprofits that aid at-risk children, subjected school library books to right-wing litmus tests and eliminated free bus rides to polling stations in poor neighborhoods. “The far-right leaders here have implemented Project 2025 on a county level,” said Alisa Simmons, a Democrat and county commissioner who is running to unseat the conservative county judge, Tim O’Hare. In an early sign this year that area Republicans may be out of step with Tarrant County’s constituents, a Democratic aviation machinist and union leader, Taylor Rehmet, defeated Leigh Wambsganss, a well-funded Republican Christian activist who led the conservative takeover of several metroplex school boards. He won by 14 points in a January special election for a State Senate seat covering a region that Mr. Trump won by 17 points in 2024. A ‘Gradualist’ Theory Which party prevails in Texas is a complicated riddle. Historically a low-turnout state — it ranked second to last in the 2024 election, ahead of only Arkansas — Texas held a primary in March that saw nearly one in four voters showing up to the polls, a modern record for midterm participation, with Democrats slightly outpacing Republicans. A few factors could conspire to thwart a blue wave in Texas. As of 2020, straight-ticket voting is no longer possible in the state, which could impact the mostly Democratic urban counties where that practice has frequently been used by voters in past elections. Texas is one of only eight states that lack universal online registration, while voting by mail is also highly restricted. In January, Mr. Abbott turned over the state’s list of approximately 18.7 million registered voters to the Trump administration, and 1.2 million of them have subsequently been put on the “suspense list” because their addresses have not been verified. The recent shuttering of nearly one-third of Tarrant County’s polling sites by its Republican-controlled county commission is particularly worrisome for Democrats. “The reason we’ve lost these statewide races in the past is because we’ve never gotten enough out of Tarrant County to overcome the margins in rural Texas,” Ms. Davis said of the turnout. “If we don’t get it to 53 or 54 percent this November, it’s game over. James and Gina can’t win.” But the state’s Republicans have reasons of their own to be fretful. Partly because of the recruitment efforts of the Texas Majority PAC and Blueprint Texas, a down-ballot candidate support organization co-founded by Ms. Davis earlier this year, the Democrats are fielding a full slate in all 150 state races for the first time in a half-century. Though many of these aspirants face long odds, their presence on the ballot could energize the Democrats in predominantly conservative regions who have not bothered to turn out in the past. “If we win on Nov. 3, most of those names running down-ballot in really tough areas like East Texas and the Hill Country and the Panhandle will be responsible,” Mr. O’Rourke said. Mr. Henson added that while he remained skeptical about Democratic enthusiasm being sufficient to carry the day for Mr. Talarico, he also doubted that a last-minute avalanche of negative ads would prove decisive for Mr. Paxton. “At a certain point, there’s diminishing impact once you get past an absurd level of spending,” he said. Rather than project a winner in November, Mr. Henson said he felt more comfortable embracing a “gradualist” theory, one in which Texas does not become blue overnight, but instead competitive. “Even if Talarico loses by a Beto-like margin,” he said, “the next cycle is a presidential election, where Trump likely won’t be popular and Democratic turnout will be higher. So there are reasons for Texas Democrats to be optimistic.”' You can unsubscribe from this mailing list at any time:

Since then, I’ve brought millions in federal funding home for public safety, clean water, and programs for young people across our district. clean_body: Don’t go to sleep on election night wishing you did more. | | | | Patriot, Don't go to sleep on election night wishing you did more. That's the standard our Turning Point Action team is holding itself to. Right now, they're all gas, no brakes, and I couldn't be more proud of them. Everything this team is doing is more than just showing up right before November, because that's not what actually wins elections. It's about building real connections while reaching voters where they are, in their neighborhoods. It takes years of preparation, with our door-knockers building relationships and earning trust. This is what my husband built Turning Point Action to do. Charlie wanted voting to become a habit for every America-loving patriot in this country, and our team is making that dream a reality, one front door at a time. Here's a look at what our team is doing on the ground right now: ✅ Hosting over 500 Super Chase events nationwide up until Election Day, activating people to chase votes in their own communities. ✅ We have trained and deployed 850+ full-time ballot chasers across key states, and the number is increasing by the day. ✅ Making sure voters in key states have a plan to submit their vote, through the work of our Chase the Vote team. ✅ Working day and night at headquarters so our field teams have everything they need to identify and reach every possible voter. ✅ Calling, texting, and writing postcards to voters, and hosting community events to get out the vote. ✅ Developing the "Freedom Ticket" as a personalized voter guide for patriots to use at the voting booth in key battlegrounds. ✅ Building permanent infrastructure in the new "Red Wall" states of Arizona, Nevada, and Hampshire. When I see this machine at work, I see Charlie's vision growing stronger across America. There's not much time left for our ballot chasers to reach every voter they can. ## VOTE NO ON ALL 3
When you get your ballot, flip it over. There are three constitutional amendments on it, and I am asking you to vote NO on all three. Question 1 would write abortion into our Constitution as a "fundamental right." It has no protection for parental consent, it allows abortion through all nine months for "mental health" reasons, and it shields providers from being held accountable. As the sponsor of born-alive legislation in Richmond, I can tell you this amendment goes far beyond anything most Virginians support. Vote NO. Question 2 would strip the definition of marriage as one man and one woman from our Constitution and write "sex" and "gender" into its place, with no protection for churches, pastors, or people of faith. Vote NO. Question 3 would automatically restore voting rights to every convicted felon the moment they walk out of prison, with no review and no exception for murderers, rapists, or other violent offenders, even while they're still on probation or owe restitution to their victims. It would also put them back on juries. Vote NO. No safeguards. No parental notification. No deal. Vote NO on all 3. Vote RED up and down the ticket: Doug Ollivant for Congress and Bert Mizusawa for U.S. Senate!

Hey everybody, my team needs to make the call on our final voter outreach budget in a bit and I'm told we're still coming up short. You can help make sure we don't need to scale back our efforts in the final hours of the campaign **[by making a donation right now.](https://substack.com/redirect/ebed4592-0f72-4e3f-8807-5ede8e432139?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
If this year feels different, **you 're not imagining it.**
Donald Trump won Ohio by a double-digit margin in 2024. But tomorrow, we're taking it back and giving working people a voice in Washington.
My opponent has spent the last two years in the Senate with real power to make people's lives better. When given the opportunity to address voters' concerns - gas, groceries, tariffs, health care - he votes to help The Money over The Many. Every time.
**That negligence would be bad enough, but I think it 's even worse.**
Jon Husted, Vivek Ramaswamy, JD Vance - and the crypto, pharma, oil, data center, and FirstEnergy guys bankrolling them - have real _contempt_ for working people.
Husted said, _we 've got to end this war_. Two weeks later, he voted to continue it. To date, he has voted 14 times to keep this war going.
He told a woman with a disabled daughter, _I will never cut Medicaid_. Two weeks later, he voted to cut Medicaid. He has voted 9 times to raise your health care costs.
Why would he tell people to their faces that he was going to do something to help, and then turn around and do the opposite? Why would he say Ohioans' "work ethic is broken"?
It's contempt.
It's not hard to know what Ohioans need and want. Husted can see it - and still he votes the other way. So now, Republicans have spent $320 million trying to convince Ohio voters that their real concerns aren't as important as whatever nasty new attack about me they're putting on the air that week.
**On November 3, Jon Husted will have to answer to Ohioans of all political stripes about the job he 's done.** Because it wasn't Ohio voters who voted for the war. We didn't vote for fertilizer prices nearly doubling, diesel going up dramatically, food prices higher than ever, gas prices, same thing. Voters didn't vote for the health care premium hikes that led to 160,000 people in Ohio dropping coverage. We didn't vote for the Medicaid cuts, or for what's happening to rural hospitals here.
Jon Husted did that. And voters know it.
We have just 1 day left. This election will be won by things we can't fully measure, like the conversations you're having with your neighbors, friends, colleagues, or family.
I want you to tell them: Help is on the way. We're going to end this war, end the tariffs, and ban health insurance companies from denying care that your doctors say you need. Tell them we're working to make it illegal for drug companies to charge them more than they do in other countries - the same pill should be the same price. Tell them I'm taking on Big Tech, Jon Husted is just taking their money.
I'm going to be out across Ohio talking to voters about the choice in this election. You've been with me and I'm so grateful. If you have time to **[volunteer with us](https://substack.com/redirect/240626b3-f9a7-4381-8693-a1e8014e2fbd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** to get out the vote, or have those pivotal conversations, or **[make a donation](https://substack.com/redirect/ebed4592-0f72-4e3f-8807-5ede8e432139?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** to keep our ads up and make sure our field operation is the strongest it can be - we're going to win.
Thank you for being part of this, and even more, for caring about all of this. It matters.
In solidarity,
Sherrod Brown

Jim Himes has represented Connecticut in Congress for nearly 18 years--almost an entire generation.
[Pledge your support](https://substack..1Ask_orXgcNWOSJINmZo8XnxD7cntz6kymGugVhPO8M?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=223185184)
My argument is that Connecticut's families face greater challenges today than when he first took office: healthcare affordability, energy costs, infrastructure, and opportunities for the next generation.
**It 's time for a new generation of experienced leadership.**
I bring a different background to this race--as a physician and attorney, with experience confronting problems in healthcare and advocating for practical solutions.
Below are my opening remarks from our second debate. They explain where I believe our approaches differ and the questions I think every voter should consider before Election Day.
> **Good evening everyone I am Dr. Michael Goldstein the Republican Candidate for Congress, I would like to thank the CT mirror for hosting this debate**
> **This debate is between myself and Jim Himes Donald Trump is not here this evening and he probably does not even know who I am.**
> **This debate is about the failures of the past in Connecticut under the total control of the Democrats**
> **We have 2 Democrat Senators 5 Democrat Congressman, a Democrat Governor and Democrat control of both houses in the State legislator.**
> **What have we gotten from this team, the highest unemployment rate in the country, among the highest taxes, almost the highest utility rates , the most congested highway in America, and limited opportunities for our children to stay and find jobs in Connecticut**
> **If Connecticut was a baseball time there would be a clean sweep but instead like drug addicts who can 't break the habit voters keep electing only Democrats knowing that they are failing the people of Connecticut.**
> **Jim Himes, will be staring in his role as Hollywood Jim in the fantasy tale of how Donald Trump will be interfering with this election with Kash Patel impounding the voting machines, federal agents with assault rifles will be at the polls and ICE agents will arrest citizens who came to vote. The real truth is that the major cheating in our elections is by democrats in cities like Bridgeport**
> **This election should be about, affordability, energy, infrastructure, the boarder, healthcare, sane immigration policies, job growth, Iran**
> **This election should be about Jim Himes failed record in helping the people of Connecticut the hundred foot congress street bridge that was never rebuilt, the hundreds of hours wasted by commuters on I95 because Himes has not raised the federal money to fix it, or the 400 postal jobs exported to White Plains so our mail can be sorted in New York and not Connecticut.**
> **Don 't forget the Democrat Socialists of America, including 3 radical socialists Mamdani congressman, and others like them. Don't forget the radical jihadists antisemite Abdul El Sayed that Even Barak Obama is looking to add to the Democrat bullpen.**
> **If you no longer want to live in a failed state you have two choices, move or elect new leaders**
> **I believe in Connecticut and if you do to I 'm asking for your vote.**
* * *
**My Closing Message**
Eighteen years is a long time to serve in Congress. It is also enough time for voters to examine the results.
The question is not simply how long someone has held office. It is what has been accomplished, what remains unfinished, and which experience and proposals will best serve Connecticut going forward.
**One generation has passed. Now we must decide what kind of future we want for the next.**
_**Please read and share these remarks, discuss the issues with your family and neighbors, and make your voice heard on Tuesday, November 3.**_
**Dr. Michael Goldstein**
Republican Candidate for Congress -- Connecticut's 4th District
Ballot Position 2B

I bring a different background to this race--as a physician and attorney, with experience confronting problems in healthcare and advocating for practical solutions. Below are my opening remarks from our second debate. They explain where I believe our approaches differ and the questions I think every voter should consider before Election Day. Good evening everyone I am Dr. Michael Goldstein the Republican Candidate for Congress, I would like to thank the CT mirror for hosting this debate This debate is between myself and Jim Himes Donald Trump is not here this evening and he probably does not even know who I am. This debate is about the failures of the past in Connecticut under the total control of the Democrats We have 2 Democrat Senators 5 Democrat Congressman, a Democrat Governor and Democrat control of both houses in the State legislator. What have we gotten from this team, the highest unemployment rate in the country, among the highest taxes, almost the highest utility rates , the most congested highway in America, and limited opportunities for our children to stay and find jobs in Connecticut If Connecticut was a baseball time there would be a clean sweep but instead like drug addicts who can 't break the habit voters keep electing only Democrats knowing that they are failing the people of Connecticut. Jim Himes, will be staring in his role as Hollywood Jim in the fantasy tale of how Donald Trump will be interfering with this election with Kash Patel impounding the voting machines, federal agents with assault rifles will be at the polls and ICE agents will arrest citizens who came to vote. The real truth is that the major cheating in our elections is by democrats in cities like Bridgeport This election should be about, affordability, energy, infrastructure, the boarder, healthcare, sane immigration policies, job growth, Iran This election should be about Jim Himes failed record in helping the people of Connecticut the hundred foot congress street bridge that was never rebuilt, the hundreds of hours wasted by commuters on I95 because Himes has not raised the federal money to fix it, or the 400 postal jobs exported to White Plains so our mail can be sorted in New York and not Connecticut. Don 't forget the Democrat Socialists of America, including 3 radical socialists Mamdani congressman, and others like them. Don't forget the radical jihadists antisemite Abdul El Sayed that Even Barak Obama is looking to add to the Democrat bullpen. If you no longer want to live in a failed state you have two choices, move or elect new leaders I believe in Connecticut and if you do to I 'm asking for your vote. My Closing Message Eighteen years is a long time to serve in Congress. It is also enough time for voters to examine the results. The question is not simply how long someone has held office. It is what has been accomplished, what remains unfinished, and which experience and proposals will best serve Connecticut going forward. One generation has passed. body:
Tomorrow, the South Sound decides.

---
| | Tomorrow, the South Sound decides. Tomorrow, the South Sound decides.

Many of you have known me since my days as mayor of Tacoma. I’ve spent my whole career working twice as hard for half as much, and I’ve never stopped showing up for Pierce and Thurston counties: helping South Sound residents navigate federal agencies, returning money to taxpayers, and securing federal grants for bridges, schools, and public health.

This is the work that drives me, and it’s the work I’ll continue to do in Congress.

So I’m asking you directly: Can I count on your vote?

Drop boxes close at 8pm tomorrow. If you haven’t registered, you can still register and vote in person at your county elections office until 8pm.

clean_body: All thanks to you. | | Peter, About a year ago, I knocked on a random door in Fairview and met a wonderful family. We talked about the challenges facing our country and the need for a different direction. A few weekends ago, that same family threw a barn party for our campaign at their lovely home. We started the year as strangers and ended it resolved to fight for the same future, side by side. | That is the pattern we have repeated across TX-03 for over a year. One door becomes one conversation. One conversation becomes a whole family supporting us. That family invites the neighbors over. Those neighbors sign up for a volunteer shift. Before long, a precinct that had never once heard from a Democrat had yard signs on every street and friends walking friends to the polls. Seats like this one flip that way, block by block. Our rockstar volunteers and staff have lived service before self through every mile of it. Nothing we are promising is revolutionary. A steady job. A roof over your head without going bankrupt. A government that stops hunting imaginary enemies and starts solving actual problems. But in the age of Keith Self’s extremism, ordinary decency became the boldest platform in Texas. The whole state is counting on us, because the stakes go beyond flipping this seat. Dave Wasserman of the Cook Political Report spent this weekend editorializing that Collin County is a must-flip for James Talarico. Our ground game is how he gets it done, and we intend to deliver this county for him. | It all comes down to tomorrow. Every door we knocked, every forum Keith Self skipped, every line around the block led here. Let’s finish what one knock on one door in Fairview started. November 2, 2026, on the eve of Election Day
**I. The claim, stated plainly**
Between the parties' closing arguments, the ad wars, the donor calls, and the surrogate armies, hundreds of people have worked this cycle to keep the Republican House majority. On the evidence, no single person did more to help them than a 25-year-old investigative reporter from the National Pulse named Natalie Winters.
On October 28, Winters published a fourteen-page election guide marked **CONFIDENTIAL** -- prepared by Protect Democracy, a group co-founded by former Obama White House associate counsels Ian Bassin and Justin Florence, and promoted to progressive state legislators by the State Innovation Exchange (SiX). It is, by any reading, the other side's operational playbook for a post-Election Day constitutional fight: seven scenarios running from Election Day through counting to certification, complete with messaging doctrine, messenger lists, and political-cost calculations.
She handed the Republican Party the enemy's war plan five days before the war. The evidence of the past five days is that the party filed it in a drawer.
**II. Who Winters is -- and why October was hers**
Winters is not a casual observer. Born in 2001, a University of Chicago graduate, she rose as a senior investigative reporter at the National Pulse and became co-host of Steve Bannon's War Room -- reportedly listened to by millions -- and a White House correspondent since January 2025, a seat she won while the press establishment worked to exclude her (her National Press Club membership bid was famously rejected). Her beat has been the stories the mainstream press buried: political corruption, national security, foreign influence.
Her October run was a sustained body of work on how the 2026 election would be fought *after* the polls closed:
\- **October 28** : "Inside the Left's 'Confidential' Playbook for the 2026 Midterm Fight" -- the fourteen-page Protect Democracy guide, its seven scenarios, its grand-jury proposals, its communications timetable.
\- **October 30** : "Inside the Anti-MAGA Plan to Count Votes Outside Government" -- the counting-week machinery.
\- War Room and Glenn Beck appearances walking millions of listeners through the documents.
Nobody else in the movement -- not the RNC's research shop, not the super PACs, not the congressional leadership's operation -- produced anything comparable in October. That is not a rhetorical flourish. It is the record.
**III. What she actually found**
According to Winters' reporting, the "confidential" guide, laid out for progressive lawmakers a "_**Deceive, Disrupt, Deny**_ " theory of a three-part administration strategy, then mapped seven distinct threats across three phases -- voting, counting, certification:
| # | The threat | What the playbook proposes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Voter intimidation | Volunteer documentation, police coordination, litigation to extend polling hours |
| 2 | Nationalized election administration | Framing it as an overreach, "label an election emergency illegitimate" |
| 3 | Seizure of ballots, machines, records | Litigation, warrant-response training, and -- in the guide's words -- "Make the escalation politically costly" |
| 4 | Criminal investigations of officials | Challenge subpoenas; educate community members to "reject improper prosecutions when serving on grand juries" |
| 5 | Interference with counting | Legal teams, observers, ballot curing, peaceful events supporting tabulation |
| 6 | Mass ballot challenges | Registration checks, provisional ballots, litigation against late voter removals |
| 7 | Refusal to certify | Litigation plus "mass peaceful mobilizations" |
And then the doctrine. The document tells lawmakers that online disinformation peaks in the _ten days before_ Election Day -- so have your messaging ready now. It tells them to amplify clergy, veterans, and business owners rather than arguing facts themselves. It says, in its emergency scenario, the quiet part with unusual candor:
"**When we fight feelings with facts, we lose.** "
And it reassures its readers: "none of these require passing a bill."
**IV. Why this was the most valuable thing done for the House GOP all cycle**
1\. Information asymmetry. House Republicans and their allies have spent hundreds of millions of dollars on television, mail, and digital. No dollar amount can buy the adversary's operational plan. Winters obtained one -- verified, documented, with a public SiX briefing trail from October 22 -- and gave it away. In the economics of campaigns, a copy of the enemy's playbook is worth more than any ad flight, because every ad flight fights a battle the enemy has already chosen.
2\. It was checkable. This was not a rumor or a leak of vibes. The guide exists; SiX publicly linked it in an October 22 briefing by its Shared Tactics & Training director, Anthony Gad. Winters' reporting gave every Republican communications office in the country a quotable, sourceable document. Whether they used it is the subject of this brief.
3\. It predicted the real battlefield. 2020 and 2022 both taught the same lesson: American elections are decided *after* the polls close -- during counting, ballot curing, litigation, and certification. The playbook's own risk chart places threats across all three phases, with a planning horizon that runs "well past the close of the polls." Winters delivered a map of that terrain five days before the game began.
4\. The timing was maximal. She published on October 28 -- inside the very ten-day window her own reporting identified as the peak information-warfare period. Whatever influence the document could have had on closing messages, surrogate scripts, and Monday-night radio bookings, the window was open.
5\. She had standing the party ignores at its peril. Winters did not merely publish; she co-hosts the most-listened-to program in the movement. The warning did not need a road map to reach the party -- it had a microphone the party controls. That the party still did not act makes the failure inexcusable, not excusable.
**V. The evidence they did not heed her**
The party built a lawsuit machine instead of a story machine. The RNC, by its own description, has fielded "the most extensive election integrity apparatus in the party's history": more than 130 election-integrity lawsuits across 30-plus states, deputy state directors in 22 states, and a record observer corps. Necessary work -- and it answers the _legal_ half of the fight. But Winters' document reveals the left's plan is the *narrative* half: make every escalation politically costly, frame every legal demand as intimidation, mobilize the public, and never -- ever -- fight with facts. Litigation does not rebut a story. Nobody in the GOP apparatus appears to have been assigned to.
The doctrine she exposed is already running. On October 30 -- two days after her report -- a federal court barred the Justice Department and DHS from pressuring election officials, threatening prosecutions, or demanding halts to ballot processing. That is exactly the scenario the playbook anticipated, and exactly the moment the intimidation framing was built to exploit. California's attorney general went on cable television to say the administration is "planting post-election loss excuses and sowing distrust." The left's story is deployed and in the field. Where is the Republican counter-story? Not on the air.
The trajectory never bent. As of this writing, the Silver Bulletin's average has Democrats up roughly nine on the generic ballot; Kalshi traders put the odds of a Democratic House takeover at 92 percent; the Cook Political Report's late-October projection has Democrats flipping between 12 and 25 House seats against a 219-214 Republican margin. Whatever the warnings changed, it does not show in the numbers.
Her reporting reached the converted and stopped there. The playbook expose traveled through War Room, Rumble, Glenn Beck, and the conservative internet -- and no mainstream outlet, no Sunday show, no network evening news treated a "CONFIDENTIAL" plan for post-election constitutional warfare as a national story. That is precisely why a party counter-offensive mattered: without the GOP making the document famous, the information war never left the right's own trench.
**VI. The counter-argument, answered**
Protect Democracy will say the guide is civic education: seven bad scenarios, a call to prepare, and -- note it -- a call to *accept the results regardless of the winner*. Run the symmetry test. If a Trump-aligned group circulated a fourteen-page "CONFIDENTIAL" guide to state legislators on fighting certification with mass mobilization, on educating jurors to "reject improper prosecutions," and on making the seizure of election materials "politically costly," it would be above the fold on every front page in America, and rightly so. The document's own language -- pre-bunking, "mass peaceful mobilizations" if necessary, "none of these require passing a bill" -- is the language of operations, not civics. Winters' reporting made it possible to have that argument in public. The party declined to have it.
**VII. What heeding her would have looked like -- and still could**
The window is nearly closed, but not shut, and the lessons outlast Tuesday:
1\. Steal their messenger list. The playbook's own research says trusted voices are clergy, veterans, and business owners. The GOP should have had those exact people on camera all week, in every battleground media market, before the counting starts -- not after.
2\. Pre-bunk, don't rebut. Every lawful observer filing and ballot challenge on Wednesday will be labeled intimidation. That label is in their playbook, word for word. Quote the playbook. The cheapest weapon in politics is an opponent's own sentence.
3\. Stand up a counting-week narrative desk. Their risk chart runs from Election Day through certification. The Republican response -- litigation dockets and observer rosters -- ends where the actual fight begins. Someone must own the story from November 3 until the last gavel.
4\. Adopt the maxim. "When we fight feelings with facts, we lose" is not just their confession; it is the instruction manual. Stop fact-checking feelings. Out-feel them: real voters, real sheriffs, real pastors, real small-business owners, on camera, first.
5\. Institutionalize the Winters function. Every cycle, one desk in the party should do nothing but read the adversary's playbooks full time -- and be answered, not managed. One person with a document and a deadline just demonstrated it can be done.
**VIII. Conclusion**
Election Day decides votes. The week after Election Day decides who governs the story -- and the story is what decides who keeps power. Natalie Winters did the only genuinely asymmetric thing done for the House Republican majority this cycle: she read the other side's playbook and rang the bell, in public, in time.
The party's answer was 130 lawsuits and zero sermon-writers; poll watchers and no storytellers; a court docket where the enemy planned a doctrine. Whatever happens tomorrow, the record is already written, and it says this plainly:
The best help anyone gave House Republicans this year cost them nothing, arrived five days early, and came with the enemy's own words as proof.
They left it on the porch.

What she actually found According to Winters' reporting, the "confidential" guide, laid out for progressive lawmakers a "Deceive, Disrupt, Deny " theory of a three-part administration strategy, then mapped seven distinct threats across three phases -- voting, counting, certification: | # | The threat | What the playbook proposes | |---|---|---| | 1 | Voter intimidation | Volunteer documentation, police coordination, litigation to extend polling hours | | 2 | Nationalized election administration | Framing it as an overreach, "label an election emergency illegitimate" | | 3 | Seizure of ballots, machines, records | Litigation, warrant-response training, and -- in the guide's words -- "Make the escalation politically costly" | | 4 | Criminal investigations of officials | Challenge subpoenas; educate community members to "reject improper prosecutions when serving on grand juries" | | 5 | Interference with counting | Legal teams, observers, ballot curing, peaceful events supporting tabulation | | 6 | Mass ballot challenges | Registration checks, provisional ballots, litigation against late voter removals | | 7 | Refusal to certify | Litigation plus "mass peaceful mobilizations" | And then the doctrine. The document tells lawmakers that online disinformation peaks in the ten days before Election Day -- so have your messaging ready now. It tells them to amplify clergy, veterans, and business owners rather than arguing facts themselves. It says, in its emergency scenario, the quiet part with unusual candor: "When we fight feelings with facts, we lose. " And it reassures its readers: "none of these require passing a bill." IV. Why this was the most valuable thing done for the House GOP all cycle 1\. Information asymmetry. House Republicans and their allies have spent hundreds of millions of dollars on television, mail, and digital. No dollar amount can buy the adversary's operational plan. Winters obtained one -- verified, documented, with a public SiX briefing trail from October 22 -- and gave it away. In the economics of campaigns, a copy of the enemy's playbook is worth more than any ad flight, because every ad flight fights a battle the enemy has already chosen. 2\. It was checkable. This was not a rumor or a leak of vibes. The guide exists; SiX publicly linked it in an October 22 briefing by its Shared Tactics & Training director, Anthony Gad. Winters' reporting gave every Republican communications office in the country a quotable, sourceable document. Whether they used it is the subject of this brief. 3\. It predicted the real battlefield. 2020 and 2022 both taught the same lesson: American elections are decided after the polls close -- during counting, ballot curing, litigation, and certification. The playbook's own risk chart places threats across all three phases, with a planning horizon that runs "well past the close of the polls." Winters delivered a map of that terrain five days before the game began. 4\. The timing was maximal. She published on October 28 -- inside the very ten-day window her own reporting identified as the peak information-warfare period. Whatever influence the document could have had on closing messages, surrogate scripts, and Monday-night radio bookings, the window was open. 5\. She had standing the party ignores at its peril. Winters did not merely publish; she co-hosts the most-listened-to program in the movement. The warning did not need a road map to reach the party -- it had a microphone the party controls. That the party still did not act makes the failure inexcusable, not excusable. V. The evidence they did not heed her The party built a lawsuit machine instead of a story machine. The RNC, by its own description, has fielded "the most extensive election integrity apparatus in the party's history": more than 130 election-integrity lawsuits across 30-plus states, deputy state directors in 22 states, and a record observer corps. Necessary work -- and it answers the legal half of the fight. But Winters' document reveals the left's plan is the narrative half: make every escalation politically costly, frame every legal demand as intimidation, mobilize the public, and never -- ever -- fight with facts. Litigation does not rebut a story. Nobody in the GOP apparatus appears to have been assigned to. The doctrine she exposed is already running. On October 30 -- two days after her report -- a federal court barred the Justice Department and DHS from pressuring election officials, threatening prosecutions, or demanding halts to ballot processing. That is exactly the scenario the playbook anticipated, and exactly the moment the intimidation framing was built to exploit. California's attorney general went on cable television to say the administration is "planting post-election loss excuses and sowing distrust." The left's story is deployed and in the field. Where is the Republican counter-story? Not on the air. The trajectory never bent. As of this writing, the Silver Bulletin's average has Democrats up roughly nine on the generic ballot; Kalshi traders put the odds of a Democratic House takeover at 92 percent; the Cook Political Report's late-October projection has Democrats flipping between 12 and 25 House seats against a 219-214 Republican margin. Whatever the warnings changed, it does not show in the numbers. Her reporting reached the converted and stopped there. The playbook expose traveled through War Room, Rumble, Glenn Beck, and the conservative internet -- and no mainstream outlet, no Sunday show, no network evening news treated a "CONFIDENTIAL" plan for post-election constitutional warfare as a national story. That is precisely why a party counter-offensive mattered: without the GOP making the document famous, the information war never left the right's own trench. VI. The counter-argument, answered Protect Democracy will say the guide is civic education: seven bad scenarios, a call to prepare, and -- note it -- a call to accept the results regardless of the winner. Run the symmetry test. If a Trump-aligned group circulated a fourteen-page "CONFIDENTIAL" guide to state legislators on fighting certification with mass mobilization, on educating jurors to "reject improper prosecutions," and on making the seizure of election materials "politically costly," it would be above the fold on every front page in America, and rightly so. The document's own language -- pre-bunking, "mass peaceful mobilizations" if necessary, "none of these require passing a bill" -- is the language of operations, not civics. Winters' reporting made it possible to have that argument in public. The party declined to have it. VII. What heeding her would have looked like -- and still could The window is nearly closed, but not shut, and the lessons outlast Tuesday: 1\. Steal their messenger list. The playbook's own research says trusted voices are clergy, veterans, and business owners. The GOP should have had those exact people on camera all week, in every battleground media market, before the counting starts -- not after. 2\. Pre-bunk, don't rebut. Every lawful observer filing and ballot challenge on Wednesday will be labeled intimidation. That label is in their playbook, word for word. Quote the playbook. The cheapest weapon in politics is an opponent's own sentence. 3\. Stand up a counting-week narrative desk. Their risk chart runs from Election Day through certification. The Republican response -- litigation dockets and observer rosters -- ends where the actual fight begins. Someone must own the story from November 3 until the last gavel. 4\. Adopt the maxim. "When we fight feelings with facts, we lose" is not just their confession; it is the instruction manual. Stop fact-checking feelings. Out-feel them: real voters, real sheriffs, real pastors, real small-business owners, on camera, first. 5\. Institutionalize the Winters function. Every cycle, one desk in the party should do nothing but read the adversary's playbooks full time -- and be answered, not managed. One person with a document and a deadline just demonstrated it can be done. VIII. Conclusion Election Day decides votes. The week after Election Day decides who governs the story -- and the story is what decides who keeps power. Natalie Winters did the only genuinely asymmetric thing done for the House Republican majority this cycle: she read the other side's playbook and rang the bell, in public, in time. The party's answer was 130 lawsuits and zero sermon-writers; poll watchers and no storytellers; a court docket where the enemy planned a doctrine. Whatever happens tomorrow, the record is already written, and it says this plainly: The best help anyone gave House Republicans this year cost them nothing, arrived five days early, and came with the enemy's own words as proof. They left it on the porch. \--- Sources: Natalie G. Winters, "Inside the Left's 'Confidential' Playbook for the 2026 Midterm Fight" and "Inside the Anti-MAGA Plan to Count Votes Outside Government" (nataliegwinters.substack.com, Oct. 28 and Oct. 30, 2026); New York Times profile of Winters (Apr. 11, 2025); Silver Bulletin generic-ballot average; Kalshi House control market; Cook Political Report projections via News18 (Oct. 30, 2026); NPR/PBS News/Marist poll (Oct. 29, 2026); Just Security 2026 Election-Integrity Litigation Tracker; ProtectTheVote.com; PBS News on 2026 poll-watcher operations.* ? Every single one of these races is winnable, Peter, but these candidates can only do it with our grassroots help.

subject: re: Trump’s Pennsylvania Tele-Rally
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Friends of Austin Davis
body:
Donald Trump will never forget Pennsylvania

| |
---

body:
Every dollar becomes two, and every dollar goes to turnout.
# [](https://ginafortexas.com/?refcode=em_ms_gh_header)[](https://ginafortexas.com/?refcode=em_ms_gh_header)
Peter,
I didn’t expect to write you an email like this again. Not the day before Election Day.
If you’ve been waiting for the right moment to make your first gift to this campaign, this is it.
Here’s why I’m reaching out. A generous supporter has just offered to match grassroots donations up to $200,000 until polls close at 7 p.m. tomorrow, for one purpose: getting every last Texan who hasn’t voted to the polls.
_**That means if we raise $200,000, we’ll have $400,000 for our final get-out-the-vote push.**_ Every dollar you give becomes two.
As of today, more than 7.7 million Texans have already voted early, and the final polls show this race separated by a point or two. We feel good about what we’re seeing. But early votes only take us part of the way. **If we come up short on Election Day, everything we’ve built together over this campaign could be wasted.**
This race is going to come down to who shows up tomorrow. So every dollar of this match goes to the work that gets people there:
→ Gas money for the volunteers and staff driving across the state to reach voters
→ Walk lists, clipboards, and literature for canvassers knocking doors through tomorrow night
→ Phone and text banks reminding voters where their polling place is and what they need to bring to the polls
→ Food and water to keep our volunteers going through long days
Greg Abbott has spent years and hundreds of millions of dollars trying to make sure Texans who are ready for change don’t show up tomorrow. This is how we fight back: door by door, call by call, text by text.
Here’s what one gift can do. Filling up a Texas-built Chevy Tahoe costs about $87.60. With the match, [**your $43.80**](https://act.ginafortexas.com/go/2683?c0=em_ms_gh_20261102_2_match.C2nrh3&refcode=em20261102-2627&t=2&akid=2627%2E299639%2EF41Oft) gift fills the whole tank for an organizer zig-zagging across town to reach voters.

| | Hello Peter,

I’ll be honest with you: I was hoping we’d raise enough yesterday that I wouldn’t need to reach out again today. You have already given so much to this campaign, through your time, your generosity, and your belief in what we’re building together in Ohio’s 8th District, and I’m deeply grateful for every bit of it.
But we came up just short, and I don’t want to leave a single voter behind.
**We need $967 to send Get-Out-the-Vote texts to 12,099 of our voter targets.**
These are neighbors who care about the issues we’ve been fighting for. Many of them just need a friendly reminder of where to vote, when the polls are open, and why their voice matters.
That works out to **about 8 cents per voter.** For less than a dime, we can help one more person get to the polls.Every gift counts:
* **$10** reaches about 125 voters
* **$25** reaches more than 300 voters
* **$50** reaches more than 600 voters
* **$100** reaches more than 1,200 voters

**Here’s the good news: if just 10 people give $100, we can easily reach our goal.** Would you be one of those 10 today?
---
| [YES, I’LL GIVE $100 →]()
---
| [I’ll chip in another amount →]()

Elections like this one are won in the final hours, by the campaigns that do the work of making sure every supporter actually casts a ballot. With your help today, we can make sure 12,099 voters hear from us before they decide whether to go.
Thank you for standing with me, for standing with our community, and for believing that we deserve leadership that shows up for us. I couldn’t do this without you.With gratitude and hope,
**Dr. Vanessa Enoch**
Democratic Candidate for Congress, Ohio’s 8th District _P.S. If you’ve already given, thank you. Forwarding this email to one friend who might chip in $10 would make a real difference too. We’re only $967 away._

clean_body: | | | = | | | Tomorrow is Election Day. If your ballot is still on the kitchen counter, don't put it in the mail. Take it to an official drop box by 8 PM tomorrow. Any drop box in Oregon will do. Then sign up at OregonVotes.gov/Track. You'll get a text or email when your ballot is accepted, and a heads-up if there's a signature problem you need to fix. Oregonians are showing up. More than a million ballots were already in by last Thursday. But I'm not going to pretend this is a normal election. The Trump Justice Department is sending federal "election monitors" into Multnomah County tomorrow. Days before the election, it sent me a letter warning of fines and prison time. They've attacked vote-by-mail, demanded voter data, and fought Oregon in court for months. They want you to doubt your ballot. They want election workers scared. And they're setting things up to challenge any results they don't like. So here's what I'll tell you: Oregon has voted safely by mail for decades. We follow the law, and we'll count every legal ballot, no matter how long it takes or who's watching. That fight doesn't end at 8 PM tomorrow. It may get harder. Results take time, and if you're counting every ballot, that's how it should be. The pressure to cut corners, cast doubt, and challenge the results will come after polls close. = = Every dollar helps me explain how important it is that every legal ballot is counted and elections are free from interference, no matter who is in the White House. Now go return that ballot.
